World.title: ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘Nasty political games’: Steele-John claims rumours were weaponised, denies taking leave Natassia Chrysanthos October 18, 2026 — 11:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Senator Jordon Steele-John has accused factions within the Greens of weaponising rumours about him for political reasons, and said he was not on leave from the party despite leader David Shoebridge saying so last week. In a near 2400-word statement posted to social media on Sunday night, the WA Greens senator responded to complaints made about him in a letter by Greens members and maintained he would take part in an investigation about its contents. “Because these references have been widely reported as allegations in their own right, I want to address each one fully and directly,” he wrote. Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge and Senator Jordon Steele-John in the Senate last Wednesday. Alex Ellinghausen “And I will explain how my experience of family violence collided with nasty political games, and why, despite what you’ve heard, I’m not on leave.”



Steele-John’s response came after this masthead reported that seven Greens members wrote to Shoebridge last week regarding “multiple allegations” about the senator’s “behaviour in the presence of women” between 2017 and 2025. This masthead also revealed the Greens had kept a 47-page dossier that catalogued allegations against Steele-John and set out ways to shut down media coverage and monitor members who raised concerns on social media. Shoebridge commissioned an investigation last week and said Steele-John was taking leave from the party room. Steele-John strongly denied the claims against him, describing them as non-specific. In his statement on Sunday, the senator elaborated with a lengthy post that said the original letter sent to Shoebridge did not detail any allegations, only said that the authors were aware that allegations existed.



Steele-John responded to three elements contained in last week’s letter before criticising the way Shoebridge handled the situation. He said that rumours had been weaponised by factions in the WA Greens who were unhappy he joined the Senate 10 years ago, and that he was not on leave as the leader claimed. The senator’s response to claims in Greens letter The letter to Shoebridge last week said Steele-John was referred to in parliament as “feels on wheels”. This masthead chose not to report the nickname in the original story. In his statement, Steele-John said he had been called “feels on wheels” by staff within parliament because he became emotional early in his career while giving speeches about the disability royal commission. “Eventually, I was informed that this phrase, which mocked my disability and my emotions, had taken on a new, more sinister meaning: that I had treated women inappropriately,” he said.



“And now, in this letter, the existence of the nickname itself is the allegation.” Related Article Greens Steele-John probe should examine Greens processes, publish key findings: WA MPs Second, Steele-John responded to a reference in the letter to an alleged incident at a Greens event in 2024 that the writers claimed had not been reported because of fears the alleged victim would not be believed. “I’m really concerned to read this. No details were provided in the letter, so unfortunately, at this point, I don’t know how I could respond, or how anyone would begin to investigate it,” Steele-John said. The third element of his response concerns allegations made about him by a woman that he had previously dated. The statement elaborated on his initial comments last week about being a victim of family violence himself.



Steele-John claimed that his original election to the Senate in 2016 had upset some Greens members “who felt that their personal political ambitions had been upended” and pressured him to resign for another candidate. He claimed those people “couldn’t move on” and recruited more members to form an unofficial faction in the WA Greens. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership How to kill a story: The secret dossier the Greens used to protect Steele-John He also said that group had heard rumours of an interpersonal conflict between him and two other people in 2017, and tried to “shop them to journalists as part of a smear campaign”. “In the lead-up to the 2019 election, the rumours resurfaced. This led to the creation of a Google Doc so that Greens staff and the party office all had the same accurate information to give anyone who had heard the rumours and was concerned. One of its main purposes was to ensure journalists didn’t bombard these two women again. Neither woman made a complaint.”



Steele-John said it was “no coincidence” the letter was sent to Shoebridge “the day after we agreed on the timeline for the next preselection”. “It is my opinion that this is an attempt to influence forthcoming party pre-selections by deliberately leaking out of context or misleading information to smear potential candidates and myself.” Steele-John says he is not on leave Steele-John said he did not ask to take leave from the party room, as Shoebridge said during press conferences last Thursday and Friday. “I very much understand the tremendous scrutiny David was under in his first week in Parliament as leader, and I have compassion for that. I also feel that he let me and my team down,” he said.



“On the morning the story was about to break, we had a series of meetings about how we would respond. I understand that he was stressed. So was I. But I feel that he used those meetings to repeatedly pressure me to say that I would take leave. I was stunned by this.” Steele-John said he told Shoebridge he would need time off to look after himself but explicitly requested the leader “not to announce that I had requested leave, because I knew it would be read as validating a story where there isn’t one”. “And that is exactly what has happened,” he said. “It was a bad call from David. We’ve all made those in politics. So, to be clear, I am not on leave and did not agree to the inclusion of that line within David’s statement.” He said Shoebridge, as federal leader, did not have the power to place a Greens MP on leave from parliament, the party or the party room. “I will continue to do my job in a way that supports my staff team, my family and my community. I believe that is what the community would expect,” he said.



“I do not know who signed this letter, and I suspect many did so out of a genuine commitment to people who experience violence. I share that commitment. That is exactly why I am so angry that it has been used this way. “When processes meant to protect victims are turned into weapons in preselection contests, everyone loses. Survivors become less likely to be believed. Real complaints are treated with suspicion. And the people who did this know it. That is not accountability. It is factionalism, and it has no place in the Greens.” Steele-John said he had “bitten his tongue” for years but owed it to the party and community to speak out against “a political clique who have now done so much harm to so many”. “I genuinely welcome the opportunity to participate in the Greens WA investigation process,” he said. “I trust it will be robust, independent and timely – and I will not be drawn into factional rhetoric that relies on distressing rumours with a total disregard for genuinely addressing the male violence epidemic across Australia.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalInterest rates RBA’s worst nightmare as oil pushes up inflation threat Shane Wright October 18, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

There are growing concerns within the Reserve Bank that the fallout from the war against Iran means inflation will remain elevated and force it to push up interest rates higher, even if it means more people may end up unemployed as the Australian economy slows. Ahead of two critical meetings in the run-up to Christmas, the bank is wrestling with the trade-off between bringing down inflation – which has remained above its 2-3 per cent target for three of the past four years – and the broader economic damage that would be caused by tighter monetary policy. Oil tankers and cargo vessels anchored off Port Sultan Qaboos in Muscat, Oman, in late June. Getty Senior sources within the bank, not authorised to comment publicly, have expressed growing concern that oil prices – which finished last week at $US106 a barrel – are showing no sign of falling as the war in the Middle East broadens to Saudi Arabia and the Gulf of Aden. While there is ongoing concern that spending by state and federal governments is also fuelling inflation, the RBA’s own economic forecasts – due to be updated next month – were based on oil prices being as much as $US20 a barrel lower.



Related Article Interest rates ‘Cost-of-living nightmare’: Consumer confidence slumps to historic low Diesel prices are much higher – around the level they hit at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war. Diesel is a major concern for every central bank, as it feeds into transport, manufacturing and food production costs. Australian inflation, which rose by 0.4 per cent in August, would have fallen but for the increase in petrol prices that month. It’s not just oil with prices for almost all commodities climbing due to the war and weather conditions. LNG prices are around $US28 per unit more than double they were before the war.



Food commodity prices are also being pushed higher, by both the increase in oil and fertiliser prices and the impact of this year’s “super” El Nino. Wheat prices have climbed by 37 per cent this year, soybeans are up by 24 per cent, sugar prices have soared by 42 per cent while cocoa beans have more than doubled. After weaker-than-expected job figures last week, which showed unemployment climbing to a five-year high of 4.7 per cent in September, financial markets sharply wound back expectations of a further interest rate increase. Ahead of the figures, markets believed there was a one-in-three chance the RBA would push the cash rate to 4.85 per cent at its November meeting. Markets now put the chance at closer to one in five. But the bank, and its counterparts overseas, continue to fret over the inflation pressures largely caused by the war and the global AI construction boom. On Friday, the RBA released papers from a conference on “monetary policy trade-offs” it held earlier this month.



Bank governor Michele Bullock, with senior RBA researcher Anthony Brassil, noted the problems caused by a supply shock to the economy such as the current surge in oil prices. They said that a supply shock coupled with the bank’s dual mandate – low inflation and full employment – meant it faced a difficult choice between supporting the economy or taking sterner action to control prices. Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock has noted interest rates could go higher if inflation pressures did not abate. Louise Kennerley “If prices are rising faster than nominal incomes, households experience a direct loss of purchasing power. At the same time, weaker activity may mean that unemployment and underemployment are already increasing,” they said. “The costs on both sides of the mandate are then visible together, and monetary policy cannot eliminate the real economic loss caused by the shock. It can only influence how that loss is distributed over time.”



The bank has already come under fire for taking official interest rates to a 15-year high of 4.6 per cent, prompting complaints that this is putting borrowers under extreme pressure. Despite higher rates, most borrowers remain well ahead on their repayments, with many holding large balances in offset mortgage accounts. In the three months to June, Australian home borrowers paid a record $21 billion in interest on their loans, but the share of household disposable income servicing mortgages is lower than in 2024, when the cash rate peaked at 4.35 per cent. But there are concerns that high inflation is doing more damage to low-income earners who are unlikely to hold a mortgage. These people have been the hardest hit by the ramp-up in rents over the past three years. “High inflation makes budgeting and planning harder, increases uncertainty and distorts price signals,” Bullock and Brassil said. “High inflation also tends to impose the most significant burdens on households with limited financial buffers.”



It’s not only a problem for the Reserve Bank. Central banks around the world have lifted interest rates over the past three months as inflation has climbed. The International Energy Agency last week noted that global diesel prices, while easing from the all-time high of $US200 a barrel reached in September, are still almost double their pre-war levels and are now starting to affect “real incomes, economic activity and inflation”. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said at the weekend that the war against Iran and the ongoing Russian-Ukraine conflict was hurting the global economy through oil prices. “Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, coupled with recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, have driven up the cost of refining crude into end products,” he said. Last week, the International Monetary Fund’s chief economist Silvana Tenreyro noted that the global economy had shown surprising resilience in the face of the turmoil unleashed by the war against Iran.



Related Article Editorial

Australian economy Tough choices needed to keep Australian economy on track for growth The Herald's View Editorial She revealed that the global economy would have been much weaker, and inflation higher, but for the re-routing of oil supplies, an increase in energy efficiency and the shift in some countries towards renewable energy. But there are concerns the ability to mitigate the drop in oil production out of the Middle East has almost run its course. A squeeze on global supplies through 2027 is increasingly expected by analysts. Tenreyro noted not only the fallout from the war on oil supplies, but the pressure being put on the world economy by the surge in activity by tech companies as they build new data centres for their AI plans. World.title: National's pledge to remove right to silence when a child is murdered 'flies in face of justice', lawyers say
World.content:
Lawyers say National's promise to remove the right to silence during child murder investigations is "dangerous" and "flies in the face of justice".

On Sunday, justice spokesperson Paul Goldsmith announced a National government would make it a Crimes Act offence for someone at the scene of a child's death not to give information to police.

Retired law professor Bill Hodge said the policy appeared to target suspects' relatives, rather than the perpetrators themselves.

"It may be aimed not so much necessarily at the primary perpetrator, but the relatives, the family members and so on, who engage in what National might call a 'conspiracy of silence'," he said.

"I'm sure the police have been frustrated, not so much by the person they see as the primary suspect, but by everyone else who was present in the house."

He said it would give police more sway during interrogations, but worried it tipped the scales too far.

"It would certainly add strength to the police arm in saying to those persons 'you must talk to us or we will charge you with this new offence'," he said.

"I think it changes the dynamic of an investigation in a way which I would say is dangerous. The investigator could now be seen to have the upper hand, given that powerful threat which they have behind them."

Professor Hodge said it also put more weight behind an interrogator's bluff.

"Investigations sometimes involve a bit of a bluff and it's quite well known that sometimes an investigator will imply somebody else, 'your so-called friend is speaking, and you may end up in trouble yourself if you don't speak yourself'," he said.

Defence lawyer Marie Dyhrberg KC said it flipped the burden of proof on its head.

Marie Dyhrberg SUPPLIED

"It's a reverse onus, it's a presumption of guilt whereby somebody who just happened to be at the location, they're presumed to be withholding evidence," she said.

"It just flies in the face of justice."

She said the right to remain silent was fundamental to a fair justice system.

"The state has all the resources and all the ability to make an allegation and prosecute someone, and the ordinary citizen doesn't have the resources to fight back," she said.

"Even if they did, it doesn't matter. You make the allegation and you have to prove it.

"You've got to recognise that sometimes proving innocence is virtually impossible. [The right to silence] is protection against wrongful conviction."

Bill Hodge said it was understandable that police and members of the public would feel frustrated by cases in which potential key witnesses had refused to cooperate with police.

"There have been situations that it upsets our conscience to have other housemates and other people in the extended family refuse to assist, and that is disturbing," he said.

"On the other hand, the right to silence is such a fundamental right. I'm just concerned about abuse by investigators. Having been an investigator myself, I'm concerned about the way they would go about an interrogation."

Despite his concerns, Hodge didn't feel as strongly as Dyhrberg.

"Put it this way, I don't think it would make me complain to the Human Rights Commission, but it's certainly something because it changes the dynamics of police and their interaction with families," he said.

World.title: Rail safety systems 'have to evolve' as concerns raised over trains running red lights
World.content:
The Transport Accident Investigation Commission has named trains running red lights as one of its top concerns.

Chief Commissioner David Clarke said the rising number of "signals passed at danger" had made it onto the agency's annual watchlist, which monitors the sector's biggest safety concerns.

"That's a train passing through a red light, in simple terms. We've seen an increase in notifications and accidents involving those sorts of incidents," he said.

"In fact, in the last three to four years we've seen four that involved passenger trains."

KiwiRail's 'SPAD' rate had doubled between 2020 and 2025, up to 3.2 incidents for every million kilometres.

That's more than triple the benchmark of one incident per million kilometres.

"As rail is evolving it's getting busier, there's more freight and passenger traffic, and as the extent of the traffic on the network increases, that increases risk. The safety systems have to be reviewed and have to evolve," Clarke said.

He said some parts of the network had engineered protections against SPADs, but not all.

"For example, in Wellington if a signal's passed at danger a mechanical lever on the side of the rail will trigger the emergency brakes," he said.

"But much of the New Zealand rail network doesn't have those engineering controls and relies on locomotive engineers seeing and reacting to signals."

Clarke said that needed to change.

"Any system that relies on humans being perfect is not a safe system - systems are safe when there are a number of layers which can capture human error or misjudgment in order that they don't cascade into an accident," he said.

World.title: Behind the push to get more young people on the electoral roll
World.content:
Who says getting enrolled to vote has to be boring?

Music, dancing, free kai and fresh haircuts are helping a rangatahi-led campaign get young people thinking about the power of their vote.

On Saturday, Ōtara Town Centre became a hub of sound system culture and community as On A Roll brought its nationwide youth-led campaign to South Auckland.

The kaupapa has been travelling to communities across Aotearoa with low voter enrolment, using music and community events to encourage rangatahi and whānau to enrol ahead of the 7 November general election.

With more than 166,000 people aged 18 to 24 not enrolled to vote, campaign director Chantelle Conroy (Te Ātiawa) told RNZ that young people have the numbers to make a real difference.

"Rangatahi, 18 to 24 year olds, are the second biggest voting population in Aotearoa, so if we could mobilise that population to get enrolled to vote, imagine the cultural, political and social landscape that Aotearoa would have."

The kaupapa has helped with more than 10,000 enrolments so far.

On a Roll has been travelling to communities across Aotearoa with low voter enrolment, using music and community events to encourage rangatahi and whānau to enrol ahead of the November 7 general election. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Bringing the kaupapa to the people

The Ōtara mobilisation was one of five stops on the Sound System hīkoi, with similar events taking place around the country.

Alongside music and performances, the event offered a way for people to connect with the campaign in a relaxed, community-focused setting.

Conroy said the goal is to make enrolment feel accessible, while reminding young people that participating in the political system can have an impact on their own lives and the lives of their whānau.

On a Roll campaign director Chantelle Conroy (Te Ātiawa) says young people have the numbers to make a real difference. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

"They do have the power and they have the power to change Aotearoa for the better and also for them and their whānau and their communities.

"It's so important to ensure that rangatahi are participating in the system to make sure that their voices and everything that is important to them and their whānau and communities are heard."

Aotearoa's first wāhine reggae sound in Aotearoa, Bigbada Boom Sound System, operated by Ariki Brightwell has been travelling the motu with On a Roll. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Sound system culture with a bigger purpose

Two of the sound systems involved in the nationwide hīkoi are Christchurch-based KAWAI and Aotearoa's first wāhine reggae sound in Aotearoa, Bigbada Boom Sound System.

KAWAI founder and operator Tūrāhui Payne (Kāi Tahu, Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Waikato), 22, said the kaupapa is about reminding young people that their voices matter.

"I think for a long time we haven't really felt like we have a lot of power. Or a lot of say at least," he said.

"Prior to this kaupapa I wasn't really someone who really cared about enrolling, to be very honest."

He said a lack of hope, alongside disruptions such as the Covid-19 pandemic cutting short his high school experience, had contributed to that feeling.

Payne said On A Roll is an opportunity to remind rangatahi they can have a say in the direction of the country.

"It's really important because it just reminds young people that we do have a say. And it is important to make sure that that's heard."

KAWAI founder and operator Tūrāhui Payne (right) says it's important to remind young people that their voices matter. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Ariki Brightwell (Ngāti Toa Rangatira, Rongowhakaata), also known as Queen Big Punch, is the founder of Bigbada Boom, which creates space for wāhine and femme artists in reggae sound system culture.

Brightwell told RNZ that music is a powerful way to connect people with wider struggles for rights and representation.

She points to the influence of reggae legend Bob Marley on Māori communities.

"As Māori, as tangata whenua, Bob Marley is a messiah to us," she said.

"He uplifted our people when we were at our lowest. He taught us that we weren't alone in the world fighting for our rights as tangata whenua as well."

Supplied / On A Roll

Brightwell said that same sense of collective strength is important when it comes to voting.

"It's important to have a say in our country. Because, you know, I think the way things go, if you're not involved, then, you have no say and can't have a part of it.

"The more people that enrol to vote, the more that can happen, the more things can shift and change to, I would say, more accurately represent the majority of our citizens of Aotearoa New Zealand."

Brightwell said a new generation was beginning to rise up, and their participation will help shape what comes next.

"Their way of thinking and their whakaaro is going to dictate the next step of our country in its direction. And I think it's incredibly important they get on the roll."

In Ōtara, a free festival called ŌRO is brought together South Auckland artists, community groups and rangatahi, with voter enrolment alongside music, kai and other activities. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

A vote for the next generation

Eighteen-year-old Charity is preparing to vote for the first time. She said young people deserved to have their experiences represented in decisions about the country's future.

"I think it's important because young people should get their voices heard, not just elders. And the elders will never know what the younger generation is going through."

18-year-old Charity is preparing to vote for the first time. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Ōtara rangatahi Pūmanawa Rawiri said voting was also a responsibility to the people and places young Māori were connected to.

"From a Māori perspective, an indigenous perspective, it's our obligation to stay connected to the whenua and everything that's happening on our whenua."

Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

Making your voice heard

South Auckland band LEAO also performed at the event, following their historical win at the 2026 APRA Silver Scroll Awards.

Their song 'LALELEI' which celebrates 'aiga ma atunu'u' (family and homeland) and captures themes of distance, yearning and commitment to the fa'asamoa (the 'Samoan way') won New Zealand's top songwriting award.

Frontman David Feauai-Afaese encouraged whānau to vote, saying it offered an accessible way for people to influence decisions that can sometimes feel distant from their everyday lives.

LEAO is the musical project of Auckland-born Samoan musician David Feauai-Afaese. Their Samoan love song 'LALELEI' made history at the 2026 Silver Scroll Awards winning New Zealand’s most prestigious songwriting award. Layla Bailey-McDowell / RNZ

"Being able to vote is an actionable and accessible way in which we can have a voice."

He said it was important for communities that were disproportionately represented in negative statistics to have a say in what they wanted for the future.

Eligible voters must enrol or update their details by midnight on Sunday, 25 October, before voting begins on Monday, 26 October.

World.title: Explainer: What are the US midterms and why are they a big deal?
World.content:
Explainer - American voters will soon get one more chance to cast their verdict on US President Donald Trump - quite possibly for the final time.

The US midterm elections are coming up on 3 November (expect results to come in after midday 4 November NZ time), and millions of dollars are being spent as candidates sprint around the country seeking votes. Early voting has already begun in many states.

But what exactly is being voted on? Here's what to look out for, and what Trump may face after results come in.

What are the midterms anyway?

They're a key part of the American political process where, halfway through a president's four-year term, voters get to pick their local congressional representatives and many senators and governors.

All 435 members of the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 Senate seats are up for election this year, as well as 36 state governors.

The midterms are usually seen as a referendum on how a president's term is going and determine whether the US Congress is led by the Democrat or Republican party.

RNZ's Tim Watkin, executive producer of podcasts and series, is a keen observer of the American political scene.

The midterms are the biggest deal for the final two years of Trump's presidency, he said.

"It will change the balance of power in America."

If Trump's Republican party loses badly, "It will give Democrats the power to question Trump in a way he's never been questioned this term," Watkin said.

US President Donald Trump delivers the State of the Union address in the House Chamber of the US Capitol in Washington, DC, on February 24, 2026. MANDEL NGAN / AFP

Explain to me again how America's Congress works?

We can try.

Instead of a Parliament, they've got Congress, which consists of two separate chambers - the House of Representatives and the "upper house", the Senate. Bills must pass both houses to become law.

The House has 435 members who are divided proportionally among the 50 states based on their population (so bustling California has the most reps, 52, while wide-open Wyoming has only one).

The Senate has 100 members and every state, regardless of size, has just two senators. The US Vice-President acts as a 101st member to break any 50-50 ties in the Senate.

The US Senate is considered more prestigious and powerful. Representatives only serve two-year terms, while senators serve six-year terms.

The current makeup of the House and Senate is very tight - there's a single seat majority in the House and six seats in the Senate. They've both been under Republican control since the 2024 election.

How big a deal is this for Trump?

Trump has operated the last two years under a Republican House and Senate and broadly exercised executive power with little pushback from fellow Republicans. That could well change after 4 November.

During his first term, when Democrats ran the House of Representatives, Trump was impeached twice, but both times the Republican-controlled Senate failed to convict him, which would have forcibly removed him from office.

US President Donald Trump speaks at a rally in Clarksville, Tennessee. ROBERTO SCHMIDT / AFP

If Democrats control both houses of Congress, look for an awful lot more talk about investigating alleged corruption, and perhaps even another go at impeachment.

While Trump has made lots of allusions to seeking a third term - which is illegal under the US Constitution - the reality is that an 82-year-old Trump probably won't be running again in 2028.

"It's Trump's last election," Watkin said.

"Once the midterm's done, especially if he loses badly, the next two years Republicans are going to be running a mile from him, and he's going to be standing there going, 'But I'm Donald Trump'."

US Speaker of the House Mike Johnson hits the gavel during a Joint Meeting of Congress in the House Chamber at the US Capitol in April 2026. SAUL LOEB / AFP

Is history on Trump's side?

Not really.

Whether or not one supports Trump's policies, history is against him.

Over the last 80 years, the president's party has lost seats in the midterms 18 times out of 20.

"A sitting president gets held to account for not achieving the promises they made a year and a half ago," Watkin said.

It's almost inevitable that any US president, by the last few years of a second term, starts to enter "lame duck" status. Trump, who has defied a lot of political gravity in his career, is racing into that timeframe.

The current New York Times average of several political polls finds Trump's approval rating sits around 37 percent.

Watkin said that a faltering economy and the impact of the Iran war have hit many Trump supporters hard.

"Those men who have been his base are now pissed off because they're now paying [US] $6 for diesel in their trucks.

"He was supposed to be the businessman."

Current predictions by the influential nonpartisan Cook Political Report and others foresee the Democrats likely to take back control of the House of Representatives, while the Senate will be a closer call.

"They've given up in the House," Watkin said. "The idea that they could hold on to majorities is gone. The Senate's the thing that people need to watch."

And of course, nobody really knows how Trump will react if his party loses badly at the midterms.

"-he will claim corruption, right?" Watkin said.

Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico with supporters at the conclusion of a campaign rally in Kerrville, Texas. BRANDON BELL / AFP

What are the big races to watch out for?

Despite all 435 seats in the House of Representatives being up for election, only a handful are truly considered competitive. The New York Times and Cook Political Report currently list just 21 seats as toss-ups that could go either way, and another 21 as leaning somewhat towards Republicans or Democrats.

Because the margin of the current majority is so slim in the House, it would take only a handful of seats to flip to give Democrats control.

The Senate currently has a 53-47 Republican majority (two independent senators caucus with Democrats), and will be harder to flip. Democrats need to win 51 seats to achieve a majority as Vice President JD Vance can cast votes to break 50-50 ties in the current House.

The Senate, with its smaller membership, longer terms and more powerful legislative powers, is key. If Democrats capture the House and Senate, Republican Trump will lose any leverage to get his legislative priorities passed. CNN has ranked 10 seats that may flip in 2026.

There are several big Senate races to watch:

Texas - Democrat James Talarico is facing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. Normally Texas is deep red, but Paxton has been dogged by a series of scandals including a fraud indictment and impeachment. Polls show Talarico doing better than Democrats usually do there, but Republicans are pouring money into what will end up one of the most expensive Senate races of all time.

Maine - Democrat nominee Graham Platner's campaign imploded and replacement Troy Jackson hasn't quite gone so viral, but incumbent Republican Susan Collins has been in office since 1997 and is in danger due to the Trump backlash.

Republian US Senator Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine. SPENCER PLATT / AFP

Ohio - A popular former senator, Democrat Sherrod Brown, is running to get back into office against Republican Jon Husted, who replaced JD Vance when he became vice president.

Michigan - One of the most combative races is between Republican Mike Rogers and progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who could become the first Muslim US senator.

Alaska - Remote Alaska would seem as Republican as they come but former Democrat Congresswoman Mary Peltola, the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, is running a close campaign against Republican Dan Sullivan.

Other important races are in North Carolina, Kansas, New Hampshire and Iowa. Many of the tight races are in states Trump won by a wide margin in 2024.

So are the Republicans doomed?

Well, we live in unprecedented times, and few political observers would've ever predicted most of what's happened in America in the past 10 years. America's deep political polarisation isn't likely to be resolved no matter what happens at the midterms.

Two big things still work in the Republicans' favour - the controversial redistricting of multiple states' congressional districts, which has seen both Republican and Democrat-controlled states trying to rejig electorates to ensure their party gets more votes. Republicans are generally seen as having created more possible seats for their party.

The second is money, which is the petrol running the US political engine. At least US$10 billion is believed to have been spent so far on advertising, by political parties as well as by big-pocketed donors such as the AI industry and Elon Musk.

Republicans are believed to still have more than US$1 billion to spend, and will pour money into places such as Texas' Senate race.

This year's election will break records, the nonprofit Brennan Center For Justice told The Washington Post recently.

"Having tons of money doesn't guarantee victory," US government ethics expert Meredith McGehee told the Post. "But the contrary is true - not having 'enough' does guarantee defeat. And no one ever really knows what 'enough' is."

And in case you're already dreading the endless carnival of the 2028 US presidential election, bad news - the race to succeed Trump will pretty much begin the day after the midterms. Expect candidates from both parties to start announcing their plans by early 2027.

Once again, when are those midterms?

World.title: The superannuation debate and the KiwiSaver election
World.content:
The Detail unpacks election retirement policies as the reality of New Zealand's increasingly costly superannuation beast starts to hit.

Audio player for " The superannuation debate and the KiwiSaver election " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/personal-finance/2008880%2Fthe-superannuation-debate-and-the-kiwisaver-election

The superannuation debate and the KiwiSaver election The Detail Download MP3 23m

If you are heading towards 65 in the next few years and dreaming of retirement, watch out.

You could be the first in more than two decades to have to wait longer.

Certainly that will be the case if the ACT Party gets its way. The other political parties are promising to keep the pension age at 65 for now, but they have also agreed to cross-party talks on retirement after the election.

It is estimated our superannuation bill will cost New Zealand an extra $3000 a minute by next decade, with warnings that costs will continue to soar as the number of older people balloons and the working population shrinks.

"The arithmetic really doesn't add up," says Generate KiwiSaver investment specialist Greg Smith, who unpacks the political parties' pledges on KiwiSaver and national superannuation on The Detail.

"You look at the projections, and the cost of super is projected to rise from around five percent of GDP today to eight percent by 2065," says Smith.

He points out that in the 1960s, seven working people paid for one retiree in Aotearoa. Now it is about four, in 30 years' there will be two workers to one retiree.

With the political sensitivity around raising the retirement age to ease the burden, Smith says politicians are focussing on KiwiSaver as the solution.

"It looks like the KiwiSaver election in many ways, certainly it's a big sub-plot," he says.

Once the election is out of the way, New Zealanders will want to see some cross-party action on retirement and some firm decisions.

"One thing that frustrates New Zealanders is uncertainty and constant change. Let's get these changes agreed, let's get them agreed cross-party and then let's stop tinkering with it," Smith says.

As KiwiSaver nears its 20th anniversary, Smith says it is time for a reset.

"It's been great in those initial sort of phases, we've got $140 billion, we've got 3.4 million members and it's made people's retirement outcomes better than they otherwise would be. It's not perfect," he says.

The average balance of KiwiSaver accounts of $40,000 falls well short of the $1 million needed for an urban couple who own their own home or live rent free, according to Massey University retirement studies.

Also, about 40 percent of KiwiSaver members are not contributing to their funds.

"There's the element that are over 65 or they're under 18 but there's also a huge element that just literally can't afford to."

Smith says the direction the political parties are taking on KiwiSaver is encouraging.

National says it will progressively move to six percent contributions for employers and employees by 2032. It favours compulsory enrolment for all newborns with a $1500 government kickstart.

Labour would raise employer contributions to six percent by 2032, but give more flexibility to workers. They could reduce or pause their own contributions while still receiving the compulsory employer payment.

NZ First is also pushing the newborn angle, with compulsory enrolment and a government kickstart of $1000. It wants to increase employer/ employee contributions to eight percent and eventually 10 percent.

ACT will gradually raise the retirement age to 67 in the next decade but keep access to KiwiSaver savings at 65. It would keep KiwiSaver voluntary but wants to remove the tax on KiwiSaver investment earnings.

The Greens and Te Pati Māori have no specific KiwiSaver policies, while Opportunity wants KiwiSaver to be compulsory with employers and employees together contributing 12 percent.

Shaw and Partners executive director Andrew Kelleher says turbo charging KiwiSaver will not only benefit retirees.

"You also create this pool of savings, which is then available for investment into the other areas in New Zealand that we desperately need, investment into the likes of infrastructure assets and other assets that will actually help us address the issue that we're trying to solve," Kelleher tells The Detail.

Kelleher says the ongoing discussion around retirement creates better understanding.

"I've got kids in their late 20s, and they certainly don't expect the National Super to be in the same format in 30 years time when they come to retire as it is now.

"It needs to be done in the next couple of years, because the longer we leave it, the less chance you've got of actually fixing the problem over the long term."

Check out how to listen to and follow The Detail here.

World.title: Baby Ru's death: Why is it taking so long to hold anyone accountable?
World.content:
This week marks three years since the killing of Lower Hutt toddler Baby Ru. National Crime Correspondent Sam Sherwood spoke with the officer in charge of the investigation about the past three years, where the investigation currently stands, and why it is taking so long to hold anyone accountable.

On Sunday, Baby Ru should be celebrating turning five with his family.

He should be getting ready to start school, meet his teacher and make new friends. Maybe he has a brand new lunch box and backpack.

Tragically, his family will be forced to mark the day without him, but not before they mourn the three-year anniversary of his death.

Thursday marks three years since Baby Ru, officially named Nga Reo Te Huatahi Reremoana Ahipene-Wall, was killed.

Speaking to RNZ, Detective Inspector Nick Pritchard, the officer in charge of the investigation which has now gone on longer than the little boy lived, says a dedicated team is working full-time to bring his family closure.

"They really want to hold those responsible to account."

Ruthless-Empire Ahipene-Wall, known as Baby Ru, died just before his second birthday, on 22 October, after being taken to Hutt Hospital in an unresponsive state. Supplied

Operation Huia

Three people were inside the Poole St, Taitā home on 22 October 2023 when Baby Ru suffered blunt force trauma so severe it fractured his skill.

The three people, who police have said are persons of interest are Rosie Morunga, her then-partner Dylan Ross, and the child's mother, Storm Wall.

Wall - who has repeatedly denied being involved in her son's death - has previously spoken at length with RNZ about what she alleges happened to her son and who she claims killed him.

RNZ is unable to report those allegations.

Neither Morunga nor Ross have spoken to the media since the homicide investigation began.

Speaking to RNZ ahead of the three-year anniversary, Pritchard said there hadn't been any engagement with the trio "for some time", but confirmed they all remained persons of interest, with police "looking at all possibilities in terms of criminal liability".

He says the homicide investigation, dubbed Operation Huia, remains active with a "small dedicated team" working full time with oversight from a senior investigating officer.

"We continue to engage with our Crown solicitor and other forensic experts. It's an ongoing situation where we're working through evidential material, assessing it and assessing the criminal liability of any persons of interest."

Asked how close police are to making an arrest, Pritchard says he can't give any timeframes.

"It's a case where we engaged with Crown quite some time ago. Like us, there's a significant amount of material that they had to review, and from that we've got some other inquiry work and forensic work that we're doing as a result."

RNZ / Mark Papalii

He says he understands how people looking in from the outside can wonder why it is taking so long to make any arrests.

He says it is "relatively common" for such cases to "take quite some time" due to the complexities involved and the large volume of material gathering during the investigations.

"Then obviously the evaluation and analytical stages we go through, seeking our legal advice for these sorts of cases because obviously we have to reach a certain threshold before considering charging any persons.

"So all of that does take time, and then as we get our case independently reviewed, then there will be things that come up that we need to do some further testing on or further work on… we are positive that we're going in the right direction, and we really want to hold those responsible to account."

Pritchard will not say whether police believe more than one person inflicted the fatal injuries, or if they have established why a piece of fabric was around Baby Ru's neck when he arrived at hospital.

He also spoke of the difficulties of a case with no "direct eyewitnesses".

"We've got a little boy who's tragically lost his life, and you know can't tell us exactly what happened… so you have to build a case around that through a wide variety of ways… it's actually building up the story through facts and evidence that can actually speak for the young child."

Asked how much police believe they know about what happened on the day, Pritchard says police have a "good picture… in terms of timeframes and obviously injuries and other aspects of the incident."

'It's not too late'

Three years into the investigation, Pritchard says the team has come a "long way", but says he has "no doubt" there are people out there who have information police need and he urges them to come forward.

He has a message for those responsible.

"It's not too late. Those persons that were responsible, or person, knows what they have done. It's not too late to actually get the conscience to come forward and do the right thing,"

"Whatever the mechanism of force used to cause that injury would have been quite significant. So for somebody to do that and actually not have the conscience to come forward is quite disturbing."

Pritchard says on the anniversary of Baby Ru's death the little boy should have been "thriving".

"It's really challenging because you think about it regularly. You think about how hard this will be, how traumatic this will be on that little boy's whanau.

World.title: A whirlwind of education change
World.content:
Erica Stanford has had more impact on the school system than any education minister in decades.

In less than three years, she has overseen the rewrite of every school curriculum, dug a grave for the NCEA qualification and mandated the structured literacy approach to teaching children to read in every primary school.

Stanford has effectively seized control of teachers' standards, excised school boards' Treaty of Waitangi obligations and increased learning support funding - and that's not even half of it.

There is also banning cellphones from classrooms, mandating an hour a day of reading, writing and maths, and accelerating the school building programme.

On top of that, there's the work of Associate Education Minister David Seymour and Tertiary Education Minister Penny Simmonds.

Between them, they've re-introduced charter schools, slashed the cost of free school lunches, brought a tougher approach to school attendance, dismantled mega-tertiary institute Te Pūkenga and moved the year of fees-free study from the first year of study to the final year.

The government now finds itself in a position of unprecedented control over the various levers that influence the school system, but has it strengthened the education system, as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon claimed earlier this year?

Stanford told RNZ there were early signs of improvement in maths, writing and five-year-olds' ability to read.

Anecdotally, there was certainly talk of improvement, especially in maths and early reading, but evidence was sketchy at a nationally measurable level.

The strongest proof came this week, with the New Zealand Council for Educational Research's analysis of the past 15 years of results from Progressive Achievement Tests (PATs). It showed maths and reading skills improved in the past couple of years, and at a reasonbly sharp rate this year.

The study also showed that, for maths and reading vocabulary, the improvement began before this government's tenure, and it did not attribute the improvements to any particular cause.

Other studies - the Curriculum Insights study of children in Years 3, 6, and 8, and the OECD's PISA tests for 15-year-olds - showed, for the most part, statistically insigificant changes.

The main area of improvement in schools that might have been influenced by the government was attendance. Last term, 64 percent of children attended regularly - the best term 2 result since 2020 and a bounceback from post-Covid lows.

Meanwhile, 19 percent of school-leavers last year had no formal qualification - one of the worst figures of the NCEA era, and likely driven by must-pass online reading, writing and maths tests introduced by the previous government.

Expecting clearly measurable changes to children's achievement from the government's actions is unfair - principals and teachers told RNZ it was too early to expect to see change.

They said schools were still coming to grips with the first of the new curriculums and many teachers continued to do things their way, until they were ready to change. Rather, this term of government has been about laying foundations.

Primary schools have worked with a new English curriculum since the start of 2025, although many shifted or started to shift to the structured literacy approach for teaching children to read under the previous government.

They've also got a new and more-difficult maths curriculum backed up by free workbooks, which is expected to bring measurable improvements in primary school maths achievement.

The remaining Y0-10 curriculums have been rewritten, with a focus on knowledge and clear progressions from year to year, for introduction next year and in 2029.

The final senior secondary curriculums are yet to drop, but the drafts are out and the government has sketched the broad outline of the qualification that will replace NCEA from 2028-2030 - exams in every subject, no mixing-and-matching of different subjects and new vocational subjects developed with industry.

Learning support funding has increased, but teachers don't believe last year's boost of $747m over four years has been as "seismic" as the minister declared at the time. The government initially raised spending by six percent and, by 2028/29, the learning support envelope will total $1.67 billion, 14 percent more than the 2024/25 starting point.

Special schools are being expanded for the first time in years and charter schools are back, with 19 open and more due to start next year.

For the most part, the charters appear to be boutique schools, but with more of a focus on neurodiverse and other disenfranchised learners than last time the model was tried. The exception is Aotearoa Infinite Academy - the online school on track to become one of the biggest.

The government has shifted control of teachers' professional standards and standards for initial teacher education to the Education Ministry.

Early childhood education regulations have been rewritten and the funding system is under review.

Independent polytechnics have been re-established as mega institute Te Pūkenga is dismantled - a change helpfully cushioned by a surge in domestic enrolments and the return of valuable foreign students.

That's a lot of change and it doesn't cover everything this government has done. In many cases, the foundations have appeared shaky.

The primary school maths curriculum was changed late in 2025, even though schools had already been using the supposedly final version for nearly an entire year.

Teachers have told RNZ that structured literacy helps more children learn the basics of reading, but some also warn that it comes at a cost to comprehension and enjoyment of reading.

Draft curriculums were condemned by subject experts and teachers as overcrowded and containing errors.

The shift to mass-provided school lunches was dogged by complaints.

Criticism has been a big feature of the government's reforms - it has not brought the school and early childhood sectors with it, and there have been remarkable levels of opposition.

Nearly every regional principals association in the country and subject associations spoke out against what they saw as badly drafted new curriculums.

More than half the country's schools publicly declared their opposition to the sudden removal of their Treaty of Waitangi obligations. Others told RNZ they shared the sentiment, but did not speak out, because they did not want to appear "political".

Nearly every education peak body opposed the government's takeover of teachers' registration and the Teaching Council standards body.

Much of the school sector's response can be characterised as backing some or even much of what the government is doing, "but not like that".

The government would have more support without culture-war moves like reducing the importance of the Treaty, omitting climate change from the curriculum in Years 0-10, only to reinstate it (sort of), and ditching the Aotearoa New Zealand histories curriculum.

There might also be more support, if peak bodies felt they had more or even some input into the government's plans. Subject associations told RNZ their members contributed to curriculum work, but could see no evidence of their input in resulting drafts.

In early childhood, many in the sector fear the current funding review will recommend watering down or removing incentives to employ fully qualified registered teachers, and decoupling their pay rates from those of school and kindergarten teachers.

Early-years teachers aren't the only ones worried about ECE. An experienced school principal warned the government's education ambitions would fail without more attention to quality in ECE.

"If you nail ECE the rest will fall into place," they said.

Despite the lack of widespread and strong support, teachers and principals spoken to by RNZ do not want to abandon the changes altogether, if the election brings a change of government.

They say the sector has been through too much turmoil and it would be better to continue with modifications than to switch horses altogether at this late stage.

They made an exception for the deletion of boards' Treaty of Waitangi obligations, arguing they were the cornerstone of equity in schools and must be restored, and the Teaching Council changes.

The Labour Party has clearly heard the same message - its policy would freeze the NCEA reforms and any curriculums that have not yet been introduced, and check with the sector how they want to proceed.

Education Minister Erica Stanford told RNZ the government had to move fast to raise achievement and close equity gaps.

"There is no time to waste when around 60,000 children start school every year," she said. "The work is not finished, but the early signs show why this government has been so relentlessly focused on evidence, implementation and getting support into classrooms quickly.

"We have made enormous change in three years, but these reforms now need time to embed and deliver their full impact. We cannot afford to put that progress at risk."

The past three years have left the school sector poised for consolidation of reforms that will lead to an unprecedented standardisation of what is taught, when it is taught, and how it is taught.

World.title: Recap: Rugby League World Cup: Fiji v Cook Islands
World.content:
The Fiji Bati have started their Rugby League World Cup with a strong win, 40-12 over the Cook Islands.

The Bati scored seven tries to the Aitu's two.

The Fiji Bati sung 'This is my Prayer' (Oqo na noqu masu) in response to Cook Islands' pre-game challenge and went on to a powerful win in the teams' pool clash in Newcastle.

Cook Islands, led by captain KL Iro, laid down the challenge after the national anthems, walking up to the Bati team as they lined up at halfway.

Api Korosau led Fiji Bati in singing their response at halfway.

On the field they managed to rake up seven tries, with Solomone Saukuru finishing with two.

It took the Bati just six minutes to get over the Cook Islands' line and score the first points of the game, with Solomone Saukuru powering over at the left corner, following a flat pass from Kurt Donoghoe.

Playmaker Brandon Wakeham slotted the ball in between the uprights to send the Fijians into the lead with six points.

Then it was Waqa Blake who beat the drifting Cook Islands' defensive line on the right, before a Wakeham bomb saw forward Jacob Saifiti climb high, collect the ball and reached over the line to plant the ball down for his try in the 29th minute.

Taane Milne and Caleb Navale got their names also on the scoresheet, as Fiji led 28-0 at halftime.

Cook Islands had their moments too in the first half, with Esan Masters directing their play.

He also pinned the Fijians on their tryline with two long restarts that forced the Bati to kick off their line twice in the first half.

Mason Teague, Makahesi Makatoa, Delahia Wigmore, Reuben Porter, and Pride Petterson-Robati tried their best to win territory and create chances against the Fijians.

But the Fiji Bati defense stood their ground and responded with their own attacks.

Safiti, Navale, Milne, Kitione Kautoga, Blake, Sunia Turuva and captain Koroisau kept the Bati running forward.

Kitione Kautoga got the Bati on the board again as the second spell started, going over nine minutes after the restart.

However, Cook Islands managed to get some good momentum in the second half and got two tries over Fiji's line.

Maui Winitana-Patelesio and Davvy Moale got two tries for the Cooks midway through the second half.

Winitana-Patelesio sidestepped his way to the tryline to score in front. He converted his own try, closing the gap to 34-6.

Six minutes later Moale ran on to a short pass to crash over. Patelesio converted, with the Cook Islands closing the gap to 34-12.

But with 10 minutes to go 21-year-old Saukuru went over for his second try when he ran on to a short pass from Donoghoe, with the Bati taking control again on the scoreboard. Wakeham pushed Fiji to 40-12 with his additional two points.

Cook Islands made a late push, playing deep in the Fiji Bati red zone but just could not get any more points.

Fiji skipper Koroisau said they knew Cook Islands would be tough and it was a good win as they kicked off their campaign in the pool of death, Pool A.

"We knew what we had to do today and we did that," he said.

"It was a great effort by the boys.

"We executed in that first half and it was a great win and pretty proud of how the boys turned up."

Koroisau said their next clash against world champs Australia will be a tougher match but they will go out to do their best.

"They are at the top of the food chain for a reason and we will go out there and put everything on the field."

Cook Islands captain KL Iro said Fiji was the better team on the day.

"Feels so good to see the fans come out to support us, we are sorry we can't put on a better performance for you guys," he said.

"Fiji were the better team today. They came out harder than we did, unfortunately that's how rugby league is sometimes.

"Very thankful to the family and aways proud to put this jersey on."

World.title: Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss
World.content:
A five-year hoodoo continues to hinder the Diamonds in New Zealand.

Since 2021, the team has been unable to beat their old foes across the ditch.

That unwelcome stat remains after tonight's shellacking in Auckland, where the hosts outplayed their shiny counterparts in every position on court.

The final score read 56-50 after a late challenge from Australia, but the margin was as great as 15 goals at one point, and that felt like a truer reflection of the game.

With a significant lead at half-time, Silver Ferns head coach Noeline Taurua rung the changes, offering opportunity to her bench players and allowing the Diamonds to work their way back into the contest.

Both teams will use the series to prepare for the 2027 Netball World Cup and have to strike the balance between winning and talent rotation.

The New Zealand Silver Ferns were very happy with their performance in game one. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

Leading into Sunday's Constellation Cup opener, the world number two ranked side was in much better shape.

Just a month ago, they stood on top of the Commonwealth Games podium in Glasgow, undefeated, to claim gold.

They'd gone through the major netball tournament without needing to face the Australians, who were on the opposite side of the draw and lost their semi-final to Jamaica, and may well have come into the series opener with some unanswered questions.

Are we as good as we think?

Would it have been a different story had we met the Diamonds in the finals?

After the way they played they should sleep well.

As their heads hit the pillow, they now know that on their day, at full strength, they are the best side right now.

Even if the official standings don't show it.

New Zealand celebrate gold in Glasgow. (Getty: Mattia Ozbot)

Their campaign at the Commonwealth Games closed the gap in the global ratings.

If they win all four Tests of the Constellation Cup, they'll dethrone the Diamonds for the first time since 2013.

"Any day to beat Australia is definitely satisfying because it doesn't come often," a pleased Silver Ferns head coach Noeline Taurua told the media.

"When we get rhythm, when we get flow and when we create, we get the speed on and we play some beautiful netball."

A lot of that hinges on the strength of Kiwi powerhouse Grace Nweke.

Nweke was still able to take the ball despite being sandwiched by Diamonds defenders. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

The 193cm tall goal shooter is only 24 years old and with the right feed from her teammates, is extremely difficult to stop.

Tonight she shot 40 goals at 98 per cent.

Nweke was ruled out midway through the last World Cup due to a knee injury, and New Zealand struggled without her up front.

They still haven't found another player that can fill Nweke's shoes. But if she's in the team, they don't need to worry.

The speed at which the ball was delivered to her in Auckland had the Diamonds' heads spinning.

Australian coaches Stacey Marinkovich and Nicole Richardson were left scratching their heads after the loss. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

Then there's the wingspan of defenders Kelly Jackson (192cm) and Karin Burger (184cm).

With 11 gains between them, they spooked the Australian shooters and held them tightly together in a pack, making it hard to break free and find space in the goal circle.

The Silver Ferns midcourt is also growing in confidence after Maddy Gordon and Kate Heffernan spent a season overseas playing Super Netball in Australia.

Diamonds' shock loss to Jamaica The Diamonds miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Brimming with confidence, the Kiwis worked seamlessly as a team to blow their visiting opponents out of the water.

It doesn't help that the Diamonds are dealing with a lot of head noise at the moment.

A difficult campaign in Glasgow followed a tough season of Super Netball for many players.

There have been shaky and inconsistent performances from the attackers.

Add in the hoodoo of playing in New Zealand, and it all fell apart. The miscommunication was rife and the team were in chase mode from the get go.

The Diamonds still made sure to celebrate Bruce's milestone with a guard of honour. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

There was no fairytale for Courtney Bruce, whose 100th cap was one she'll be hoping to forget.

Both she and captain Liz Watson — the two centurions in the current group — ended up being pulled off to finish the game.

"That never happens, aye," Tarurua remarked.

The one positive was the debut of 23-year-old South Australian Jessie Grenvold after a phenomenal domestic season.

Injected in the second quarter, Grenvold finished the game with more gains (three) than any other Diamond.

Still, head coach Stacey Marinkovich defended her veterans, insisting the changes that saw them head to the bench were about connections rather than individual performances.

Jessie Grenvold finished with three gains, more than any other Diamonds player in her debut. (Getty: Fiona Goodall)

"At the end of the day we were looking at different combinations and what could other people do," Marinkovich said.

"Jessie's here for a reason and we only have four games before the World Cup so if I don't get players out there I'm not going to know what they can do against international opposition.

"We switched things around, it's not to discredit our senior players we just need to trial other things."

Marinkovich highlighted the need to improve now there were more New Zealand imports than ever before playing in the Australian competition.

NZ imports flock to Super Netball ahead of Comm Games Nine Kiwi players will feature in Super Netball for 2026, after the New Zealand governing body relaxed its national selection policy. But just like the green fruit, their influx has left a sour taste in the mouth of rusted-on Australian Diamonds fans.

"There's not doubt Super Netball has shown them what to do in pressured moments on a regular basis ... That is the reality of it now."

"I don't know if we were a bit tense coming in but that's the thing coming to New Zealand off the loss of the Commonwealth Games.

"We need to process that and work our way through what that experience was and how do we get our connection out on court."

A game review will likely find that 15 substitutions in the middle quarters was too many for the losing team.

Although substitutions were definitely needed, whether the right ones were made at the right moments is the finesse that was probably lacking in the game plan. As was the fortitude to beat at team at the peak of their powers.

The Diamonds were missing Kate Moloney in the centre position and are hoping the vice captain will be available for the second Test after suffering a finger laceration at training.

The next game takes place on Wednesday night in Christchurch.

Relive all the action from the Constellation Cup in the blog below.

World.title: Animal welfare group calls for accountability after latest racing death
World.content:
Animal welfare campaigners have called for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths after Ohope Wins was put down following a fall in the Caulfield Cup.

The Chris Waller-trained Ohope Wins was in the finishing straight of the 2,400m Group One race when it was brought down by last year's winner, Half Yours, which had fallen at the 300m mark.

Half Yours got up and ran riderless down the straight, while Ohope Wins was assessed by vets as it lay on the track and was euthanased.

Half Yours received lacerations and abrasions after falling in the Caulfield Cup, but got up and ran to the finish rider-less. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Half Yours's rider Mark Zahra and Ohope Wins's jockey Jye McNeil were taken to hospital for observation.

Racing Victoria confirmed Zahra was released on Saturday night, and McNeil would be released on Sunday, with both jockeys escaping serious injury.

Racing Victoria stewards will hold an inquiry into the incident, although a time has not been set for this to happen.

Ohope Wins euthanased after Caulfield Cup fall A Racing Victoria track veterinarian euthanases New Zealand mare Ohope Wins after a shocking fall in the Caulfield Cup that included 2025 Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours.

The Coalition for the Protection of Horses campaign director Elio Celotto said at least 160 horses have been killed as a result of injuries sustained in racing across Australia this year.

"When a horse falls their legs are very delicately poised when they hit the turf," Mr Celotto said speaking to ABC's News Breakfast.

"They're a half a tonne horse and all they need to do is fall slightly off and it can result in damage to their bones and that is why we see so many horses killed on our race tracks."

He said the racing industry was responsible for deaths on race tracks.

"The racing industry has got a lot to answer for. They say they are open and transparent, they are anything but," he said.

"They really need to be made accountable for the thousands [over the years], not just the horse that was killed yesterday, but all the horses that are killed around Australia simply to make money and for the pleasure of punters. It's simply not acceptable."

Top racing trainer Peter Moody defended the industry, saying that safety improvements had been brought in since a series of deaths in the Melbourne Cup beginning more than a decade ago.

Moody told ABC Radio Brisbane there were less incidents in major races following the changes, including what he called "stringent protocols" horses go through before they are allowed to race by authorities.

Most of the deaths in the Melbourne Cup were standalone incidents, where horses broke down while running rather than colliding with or falling over other horses.

Racing Victoria requires all international horses coming for major races to have one CT scan of the distal (lower) limbs to identify possible bone damage before travel. They then must have a standing CT scan before every start in the Spring Racing Carnival.

There have been no further deaths in the Melbourne Cup since the introduction of scanning requirements.

Mandatory scans for Melbourne Cup runners A diagnostic scan on racehorse Anthony Van Dyck may have picked up on the potential for more serious injuries before his ill-fated run in the Melbourne Cup, a review finds.

Moody described the incident at Caulfield as "very sad and very disappointing".

Moody was asked if there was any way such incidents could be avoided when big fields of horses were running around.

"Whether there were some misjudgements, some horses rolled around in the race, it got tight, one horse (Half Yours) stumbled and dislodged the rider, and then the second horse unfortunately got tangled in that horse and fell also," he said.

"It's just one of those unfortunate accidents. No-one sets out for that to happen. Everyone wants to see the horses and the riders come home safely.

"The love and care and attention [given] to these animals is second to none.

"Unfortunately in all walks of life, whether it's horse racing, a football match, walking across the road to catch a bus and accidents do happen."

World.title: 'Outstanding' Tonga puts England on the brink of World Cup elimination
World.content:
Coach Kristian Woolf says Tonga showed off its new-found "depth and quality" in marching past England at the Rugby League World Cup.

The result left the English at risk of missing the semifinals for the first time.

With His Majesty King Tupou VI and Crown Prince Tupouto'a 'Ulukalala among the sellout 18,302 crowd in Perth on Saturday night, Tonga controlled the game when it counted, for a 30-12 win.

"We got more and more confident. What I liked the most was the way we defended; we put ourselves under pressure a couple of times, but our defence was outstanding," Woolf said after the game.

"You could see how much the game meant to us, and we showed that in our effort, and it's something that will carry us through the tournament."

The Mate Ma'a got better as the game went on, powering away from the world number three side to seal a victory which puts them in the box seat to reach the semifinals.

Kangaroos halfback's World Cup over Mitchell Moses will play no further part in Australia's Rugby League World Cup campaign after suffering a calf injury.

A first-half try to Stefano Utoikamanu set up a 10-0 lead at the break. But an early score from AJ Brimson was quickly countered, with two tries to Haumole Olakau'atu and one from Tolutau Koula asTonga ran away with the game.

A try to Dominic Young with under 20 minutes to go was only a consolation for England.

"We've done some special things with the Tonga team, but we're still quite new to beating tier-one nations, and England are that – they're a very strong team. We knew they would come out and be physical, and challenge us in different ways," Woolf said.

"It's a continuation of a journey that we're on. If you look at some of the young guys and some of the guys who are a little bit more experienced now, the experience they've got over the last three or four years has been outstanding.

"It's put us in a really good position. They're getting better and better. We've got depth and quality, and we can go and do something with it now."

Team Tonga took their bows to the big crowd in Perth after wrapping up a vital win over England. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

The defeat is a huge blow to England's chances.

England (or previously Great Britain) has never failed to reach the final four at a Rugby League World Cup.

This result leaves Brian McDermott's team likely to fall short, given the format of the competition.

The team was playing for the first time since losing to Australia in Leeds in November last year.

"It was a really good contest, and when it wasn't a contest, that was probably more to do with us in the errors that we made," McDermott said.

"They're a big team, strong team, and they've got some tremendous players in there. And I thought we we stuck toe-to-toe with them for nearly all the game."

England has to beat France on October 24 and Papua New Guinea on October 30 and hope other results and scores go their way, as they try to finish in the top two of the combined six-team Pool B and C.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

With Samoa opening its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, it leaves England needing to post massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Renshaw to stay at number five as Aussies delay naming Test side
World.content:
Matt Renshaw is set to remain at number five for the second Test against South Africa, as Australia waits on the opening day's weather to name the team.

Captain Pat Cummins confirmed on Saturday he expected Renshaw to again bat in the middle order after his match-winning heroics in Durban.

That all but ensures Nic Maddinson will stay in the side and open with Travis Head, after scores of 0 and 48 on his shock Test recall last week.

Renshaw's scores of 190 and 82 came after he'd originally been recalled as an opener in Australia's previous Test against Bangladesh, the position where he has batted for most his career.

Test win silences critics Australia started the first Test against South Africa on the back foot, but its 214-run victory has silenced any critics of the selection strategy.

"After what Renners did last week, I presume he'll stay at number five," Cummins said on the eve of the Gqeberha Test.

"What he deserved even more credit for is that we'd asked him to do a different role, and he just said straight away, 'Yep, no worries, whatever the team needs.'

"So many positives in addition to the runs he scored last week. He was a delight, and really helped me and [Nathan] Lyon get through those partnerships."

Cummins also confirmed Cameron Green remained sidelined with an abdominal strain, while Josh Inglis was close to being declared fit.

Josh Inglis is unlikely to return despite recovering from a fractured finger.

Even if Inglis is cleared to play following his fractured finger, it is unlikely he will be able to force his way into Australia's side.

Rain is expected across the opening two days in Gqeberha, with the prospect that both sides will be able to factor that into their XIs should the toss be delayed.

That could potentially reduce the need for spin and provide the option of a fourth quick in Scott Boland, with extra grass also left on the St George's Park wicket.

Depending on the weather in Gqeberha, Scott Boland could get one of his rare chances to break into the Australian side. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor, file photo)

But Cummins gave every indication that Lyon would remain as a key part of the attack.

"We always look at all options," Cummins said when asked if it was conceivable that they could go in without a specialist spinner.

"We love playing with Nath. We saw last week, a couple of key wickets in the first innings.

"And even the control he gives. It makes the rest of us fast bowlers be able to function around him."

AAP

World.title: Is New Zealand holding back women's Test cricket?
World.content:
For years fans and players have been crying out for more women's Test cricket.

Yet by the time Australia's women next don the whites at Headingley to kickstart the 2027 Ashes, 15 months will have passed since their last red-ball match.

Much of this comes down to the team's limited opposition. Just four of the top-ranked women's teams have cricket boards willing to commit to Tests.

Australia, England, India and South Africa have been pushing forward the past five years.

They've played 13 Tests since 2021, either as a standalone or part of a multi-format series, a significant improvement on the five years prior when two Tests were played worldwide.

Both of these fell in the 2017 and 2019 Ashes. The biennial contest has safeguarded tradition for England and Australia at a time when governing bodies have been hell-bent on growing the women's game through the shorter formats.

Australia and England play one Test as part of each multi-format Women's Ashes series. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

In fact, the Ashes points-based system used to determine the better side across three T20Is, three ODIs and a single Test, has widely been suggested by administrators and players as the best way to increase women's Tests overall. Enticing those on the fence to give it a go.

Tacking on a four-day Test match to a tour that already features six white-ball fixtures sounds like a no-brainer.

Unfortunately, two countries have knocked back that idea this year.

Australia missed out on a chance to face the West Indies in a Test for the first time in 50 years in March when their plans to play a multi-format series in the Caribbean fell through.

Then New Zealand declined to play a Test against Australia later in the year.
