The three T20Is and three ODIs scheduled between the trans-Tasman rivals were originally supposed to run through February and March, but when the ICC's inaugural Champions Trophy shifted on the calendar, the tour had to be split.

Instead the three T20Is will now be played at North Sydney Oval, starting Sunday, while the ODIs will still be played at the end of the summer.

The White Ferns are currently in Australia to play three T20 internationals. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

As close neighbours, the White Ferns would be ideal opponents for regular Test match cricket. Both in proximity and habit, the sides already meet most seasons for the Rose Bowl series.

Sadly, New Zealand Cricket doesn't share that view.

Despite being one of the first three nations to play women's Test cricket in the 1930s, it now refuses to play the longest version of the game.

Limited overs prioritised

The summer of 1934–35 saw the birth of women's Test cricket, when Australia and New Zealand hosted England on its first overseas tour.

Now, the White Ferns haven't played a Test since 2004.

After the governance of the men's and women's sides of the game were amalgamated, the frequency of Tests for the White Ferns gradually decreased and have now been non-existent for 22 years.

It also appears New Zealand Cricket is unwilling to budge on the matter, as per their previous statement in the media:

"The limited-overs formats have proven to be very effective in terms of attracting and retaining young players, which is a significant factor in the health of the women's game here. "In time, this will provide a bigger base from which talented players will emerge to ultimately play for the White Ferns. "Focusing on formats which include ICC global events, such as World Cups, is our preference for now."

ABC Sport requested a fresh response and more clarification but did not hear back.

That means retiring Kiwi legends Sophie Devine, Suzie Bates and Lea Tahuhu never got to experience red-ball cricket internationally.

At the end of the T20 World Cup the trio retired.

The New Zealanders warmed up for their T20Is in Australia with a clash against the Governor-General's XI. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Various Australian players told ABC Sport it was an "atrocity" and a "real shame" that after 15 to 20 years of service the trio weren't offered the opportunity.

"Those girls are absolute icons and to think that they've never played a Test match and never will, knowing that they want to, that's tricky," Australia captain Sophie Molineux said.

"Hopefully one day we can play another Test against New Zealand, that would be really special."

"It's a tragedy that they won't get a baggy black cap," Beth Mooney said.

"I feel really sorry for them," Ellyse Perry added.

"They've had amazing, decorated international careers and never got to experience it."

Equal pay to blame

In 2022, New Zealand Cricket was heralded for a groundbreaking pay deal that granted men and women equal match fees.

From then on, when representing their country, both sets of athletes would be paid $NZ4,000 ($3,245) per ODI and $NZ2,500 per T20I.

Although this five-year agreement, due to expire next year, was a positive step in the recognition of female cricketers, it seems to have put the final nail in the coffin for Tests. Requiring a fee of $NZ10,250 per player, it pushed the dream further out of reach.

Especially in light of New Zealand Cricket's latest budget update, which predicted a $NZ7.3 million deficit for the past financial year.

New chief executive Geoff Allott started in the role in July and has indicated the organisation will need "to be prudent" as it looks to get back on track and "ensure long-term sustainability" of the game.

Tahuhu, Devine and Bates made history as New Zealand won its first T20 World Cup in 2024. (AP: Altaf Qadri)

White Ferns head coach Ben Sawyer recently finished up a four-year tenure where he took the team to its maiden Women's T20 World Cup victory in 2024 and a bronze medal at the 2022 Commonwealth Games.

Speaking with ABC Sport, Sawyer highlighted the financial burden and the recent news that the England and Wales Cricket Board is considering footing the bill for its April Test match against the West Indies in order to ensure their 2027 multi-format series goes ahead.

"The reality is that it's a very expensive venture because of the equal match payments in New Zealand, and the cost is a huge part of it," Sawyer said.

"I'm assuming that's over $NZ150,000 in match payments and there are other priorities for them.

"Their domestic structure isn't full-time, and so it's my opinion that they think that money could be better used elsewhere."

Sawyer has previously held a range of coaching roles in women's cricket — as an Australian assistant, the head coach of the Sydney Sixers and the head coach of the Birmingham Phoenix.

Ben Sawyer has held several high-profile coaching roles in women's cricket. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He explained that New Zealand's top players are only contracted from October to March for eight hours per week. They train individually in the off-season and with teammates in-season at night after work.

When Sawyer first took on the White Ferns job, he recommended the national sporting body copy England's county system and gradually build their numbers the same way; starting with two to three professionals in each county, before eventually signing five to seven and then making the entire team full-time.

Since then, he hasn't seen any progress in this regard.

"I've always respected the vision that Cricket Australia have for five to 10 years down the track and the money they're willing to invest; that's what makes them the best in the world," he said.

If New Zealand Cricket was to change its mind and green-light a women's Test, Sawyer believes it'd be better to play someone with a lower ranking and a similar part-time domestic structure.

"They'd need a good lead in, and I wouldn't necessarily want to play Australia first.

"Maybe that's where two countries like New Zealand and Sri Lanka get together and say let's play one.

"I've got no doubt it'd be tough and hard the first time, but it's the only way to get better."

This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

World.title: Meet the first hijab-wearing non-verbal wheelchair basketballer
World.content:
It was the speed and adrenaline that first attracted Reema El Qassem to wheelchair basketball.

After two years in the game, she is regarded as one of the best up and coming players in the Women's National Wheelchair Basketball League.

Not only extremely talented, El Qassem is the first non-verbal and hijab-wearing player on the court, challenging the notion of who belongs in the game.

"I feel the most alive and the most able when I'm playing sport," El Qassem told ABC Sport.

"For those moments, I'm not thinking about my disability; I'm just an athlete."

Reema El Qassem plays for the Sydney Uni Lions in the National Wheelchair Basketball League. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

El Qassem's journey has been a difficult one; she acquired her disability, Functional Neurological Disorder (FND), in 2023.

The condition affects how the brain and nervous system function, leading to a variety of neurological symptoms, including walking and speech difficulties, cognitive issues, and chronic fatigue.

After spending 320 days in hospital and taking eight months to adjust to life as a wheelchair user, sport was the pathway to normality for El Qassem.

"When the doctors told me I would be going home in a wheelchair, I remember thinking, that's OK, I'll just play wheelchair basketball," the 35-year-old said.

"Finding sport again after acquiring my disability felt like finding a part of myself that I had lost."

It's been a meteoric rise in the sport for El Qassem, who plays for the Sydney Uni Lions, with the team making it to both the 2025 and 2026 national league play-offs.

Paralympian Hannah Dodd is coach of the Sydney Uni Lions and a mentor for Reema El Qassem. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

In recent years the women's game has been actively rebuilding across the country, adding three new teams to the national league in 2025.

Sydney Uni Lions player and coach Hannah Dodd believes this growth is what has supported the development of players like El Qassem.

"She's naturally got a really good push on her, and she's got naturally some good speed on her, so we've just been teaching her how to control it and how to use it successfully," Dodd said.

"It's just teaching her the patience and the finesse of things."

It's not just the team that is teaching El Qassem; in bringing her disability and faith to the court, she is showing the league that anyone can play.

Muslim women face additional barriers

Muslim women can face many barriers in sport, such as uniforms that don't meet modesty needs, discrimination and inflexibility around religious and cultural practices.

Reema El Qassem's community, including her four daughters, often turn up to support her at national league games. (Supplied: Wheelchair Sports NSW/ACT)

This has made El Qassem's journey into wheelchair basketball even more remarkable as the first ever player to wear a hijab on the court.

Marta Myhill, from Wheelchair Sports NSW, said El Qassem was helping those around her learn about her culture and faith.

"In her bringing her culture, wearing her hijab, there's not a problem with that at all," Myhill said.

"Everybody within the wheelchair basketball community has embraced her."

From her teammates reminding her it was time to pray, as well as notifying officials and players that they can't shake her hand, the support has almost bought El Qassem to tears.

"Growing up, I spent a lot of time trying to shrink myself and be subtle because I was always scared to draw attention," she said.

"To be so outwardly me as a Muslim woman and feel safe and welcome to practise my faith is something I don't take for granted."

Another key part of El Qassem's life is being a single mother to four daughters, some of whom also have additional needs.

Balancing her sport, faith and family can be a challenge.

The single mother of four daughters wants to show what is possible for other Muslim and non-verbal women in sport. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"There is always that guilt when I leave them, when I fly interstate, or when I come home from sport and I'm too tired for them," El Qassem said.

"There were so many times when I considered leaving the sport completely because I felt like I was being a bad mum for choosing myself."

As a mother, it has been important for El Qassem to show her children what people with disabilities are capable of.

Loading Instagram content

They have become her biggest supporters, with El Qassem taking them to cheer her on at national league games.

"It [wheelchair basketball] gives them an environment where they can admire other people, appreciate what they have, and understand that life isn't over because someone has a disability or because something difficult has happened to them," El Qassem said.

"Now they see the person, they see the athleticism, the speed, the talent, the strength, and the determination, and for me, that is such a beautiful thing for them to experience."

Non-verbal El Qassem team's 'loudest player'

Naturally very expressive, El Qassem relies on body language and facial expressions, alongside her phone app, to communicate with her team on and off the court.

So much so, last season she won the Uni Lions team award for the loudest player.

But the technology on her phone can be fiddly to use and doesn't quite cut through the ambient sounds during a game.

Generally, Reema El Qassem uses a phone app to communicate, but this doesn't work when on the court during a game. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"I can't call out that a pick is coming, call for help, or yell out to my teammates that I'm open," she said.

"Those are all things I would normally be communicating on court.

"I'm starting to see and understand the game as a whole, rather than just my own role and that has made me much more aware of the impact of being non-verbal."

Embracing the challenge with gusto, the Sydney Uni Lions have trialled different tools to help El Qassem communicate with her teammates, including talking buttons.

Unfortunately, these were not loud enough for game days when fans were cheering from the sidelines.

They are also contemplating trialling an air horn of some kind, which she could bump with the side of her leg, but the search for an effective solution is ongoing.

"Having a player like Reema has obviously been a new experience for all of us and a new way to figure out how to play a very verbal sport, non-verbally," Dodd said.

"A lot of the time we'll pair [Reema] up our most experienced pointers, to help her navigate, so she has someone that will talk to her constantly."

The Sydney Uni Lions wheelchair basketball team has been working with Reema El Qassem to figure out a way for her to communicate on court. (ABC News: Scott Preston)

Despite occasionally feeling frustrated having to rely on her team this way, El Qassem appreciates the community and friendship she has found with the Lions.

Being in a safe and supported environment has enabled her to focus on developing her potential and set her sights on representing Australia one day.

Getting classified to play at an international level, however, has proven her biggest barrier in the sport yet.

The role of classification is to make Para sport as equal and fair as possible for all athletes, but in recent years there have been some changes that have affected newer athletes like El Qassem.

Unfortunately, her impairment, FND, doesn't fit within eligibility requirements for the sport.

Reema El Qassem dreams one day of playing for Australia in wheelchair basketball, but faces an uphill battle to be classified. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"The problem isn't that the disability isn't real, it's that the current classification system isn't designed around [it]," El Qassem said.

Unable to be classified for international competition means that El Qassem is limited to playing within the national and local league seasons.

"There is not a lot of competition available for us in Australia; even our national league only runs for three months of the year," Dodd said.

"[It's] trying to get game time for the developing players, in a space where they're comfortable and where they are going to succeed and not get frightened or stressed."

Representation and belonging key: El Qassem

While El Qassem may be locked out of international competition, it's her cheerleaders at home that make the game worth it, including retired Paralympic wheelchair basketballer Gerry Hewson.

Reema El Qassem is working with retired Paralympian Gerry Hewson to improve her skills. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

El Qassem has brought Hewson on for one-on-one training with the focus on building her skills, with Hewson taking her through her drills each week.

Hewson says her determination is unbelievable.

"She's on a big learning curve at the moment," he said.

"For me as a coach it's just kind of building her self-belief that she can play at a national league level and that's what I'm trying to help her out to do."

And while the dream of representing Australia one day is still there, for El Qassem it is the community she has created and the pathways she is carving out for athletes like her that keep her in the sport.

Reema El Qassem wants to see more Muslim and non-verbal women participating in sport. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

"For Muslim women living with disabilities, I think representation and belonging are particularly important, and we deserve to see ourselves in sport too," she said.

"I also love how sports bring people together. It doesn't matter what your race, ethnicity, background or mobility is, everyone has a place, and everyone belongs."

World.title: Wallaroos not content with simply being 'better versions' of themselves
World.content:
Among Siokapesi Palu Sekona's many impressive qualities as Wallaroos captain is her uncompromising approach.

Wallabies outclassed by All Blacks The Wallabies fall to the All Blacks for the 13th straight time, as their trans-Tasman rivals record a convincing 43-21 win in Sydney.

As such, it does not come as a shock to learn she feels the Wallaroos still have much room for improvement following their dominant 56-12 win over Scotland in this afternoon's Global XV Series Test.

The eight-tries-to-two victory did not represent a complete performance in Palu Sekona's eyes, which should serve as music to the ears of Wallaroos supporters.

Why?

It shows the Wallaroos are setting the highest possible standards for themselves.

"We still know there is room for improvement and we definitely know what to do to clean that up," Palu Sekona said.

Wallaroos skipper Siokapesi Palu Sekona put in a solid shift on both sides of the ball. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Wallaroos defeated Scotland 30-10 three weeks ago in Edinburgh during their three-Test swing through Great Britain and France as part of the Global XV Series.

The victory snapped a six-match losing streak but left Wallaroos players and coaches dissatisfied.

It was a sign of the Wallaroos' quickly developing harder edge, which Palu Sekona wants carried through to the 2029 Women's Rugby World Cup.

"We knew we could put together a better performance," she said.

"Ultimately results and scores are what people look at. But if we want to break down our rugby, there are so many things to clean up.

"From discipline, to our ruck, to the accuracy of our set-piece. There are things we can continue to work on."

Wallaroos set bar high

The Wallaroos, ranked seventh in the world, are starting from behind scratch when compared to teams such as England and New Zealand.

Both enjoy the benefit of being full-time programs, with their respective governing bodies making a wise move to invest in the women's game.

The Wallaroos are still semi-professional, but a shift to full-time status — as part of an integrated program alongside the women's sevens squad — is in progress.

There is no doubt the Wallaroos' rate of improvement will be accelerated once they go full-time in the lead-up to the World Cup, which Australia will host.

"We don't want to only be the better versions of ourselves," Palu Sekona said.

" We want to be the best in the world. "

Winger Amelia Whitaker scored a double in the Wallaroos' victory. (Getty Images/Corbis: Steve Christo)

The Wallaroos' makeshift coaching team, under the leadership of Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh, has had a positive influence on the playing group.

Sione Fukofuka will take over as head coach next year and work alongside Walsh, who enjoyed tremendous success in charge of the Australian women's sevens squad.

Like Palu Sekona, Walsh was not completely satisfied with the Wallaroos' display against Scotland.

But he saw enough to know they are heading in the right direction.

"I think it was another step forward, for sure," Walsh said.

The Wallaroos will complete their 2026 Test season when they meet Scotland in Canberra on Friday night.

World.title: World Cup heartbreak for Kangaroos half as Tonga notches first win over England
World.content:
Mitchell Moses will miss the remainder of the Rugby League World Cup, after being ruled out of the Kangaroos' title defence with a lower leg injury that continues his representative misery.

The Parramatta playmaker suffered the injury during Australia's 24-22 win over New Zealand in the tournament opener on Thursday night in Sydney.

He attempted to play on but eventually left the field less than two minutes into the second half.

Meanwhile, England's hopes of reaching the World Cup semi-finals are already on life support after suffering a 30-12 loss to world No.5 Tonga in their blockbuster showdown in Perth.

Moses was injured during the Kangaroos' World Cup opener against New Zealand. (Getty Images: Matt King)

While initially believed to be a calf issue or a hairline fracture, scans following the match revealed Moses had suffered an unspecified "high-grade muscle tear", meaning his World Cup campaign is over.

It's a blow to the Kangaroos, who are already missing Nathan Cleary with a serious leg injury, with Moses the Kangaroos' strongest last-tackle kicker.

Moses switched allegiance to play for Australia at this tournament after captaining Lebanon at the 2022 World Cup.

In Perth, Tonga produced a defensive masterclass in its four-tries-to-two victory over England.

The result put Tonga in the box seat to reach the semis, with games against Lebanon and Samoa to round out the group stage.

England's World Cup campaign is already on life support after Tonga's statement win in Perth. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

In contrast, world No.3 England have been left on the brink of elimination — even if it wins its remaining two games against France and PNG.

Under the confusing group stage system employed for the World Cup, only two teams from across pools B and C will progress to the last four.

If England finish on the same number of wins as Tonga, then Tonga will go through given they won Saturday's head-to-head battle.

World Cup opener a reminder of Australia's glory days There was a time when Test matches were rugby league's biggest, best and bloodiest spectacles, and last night's World Cup opener between Australia and New Zealand was a reminder of those days.

Should England and Samoa end up with the same number of wins, the tiebreaker will be which nation has the better points-for-and-against differential.

Samoa opened its campaign with a 78-4 smashing of France, leaving England needing to post some massive wins in its remaining two games to stay alive.

Stefano Utoikamanu opened the scoring in the 24th minute when he found a hole in England's defence to stroll over untouched.

A pair of Isaiya Katoa penalty goals extended the margin to 10 points by half-time, with England left to rue a series of fumbles and near misses.

England started the second half full of steam, resulting in a team-lifting try to AJ Brimson in the 46th minute.

But in a game where hard work was king, it was a slice of fortune that ended up giving Tonga a vital edge with Haumole Olakau'atu scoring the first of his two tries after he soccered the ball into an opponent's arm and then gathered the bouncing rebound.

And when Tuimoala Lolohea's neat dribble found Tolutau Koula in the corner to make it 22-6 in the 58th minute, it was as good as game over.

The win was a powerful statement from Tonga, whose only previous taste of international success against England came in 2019 when they beat Great Britain.

In Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea's men's side earned a gritty 42-18 win over Lebanon hours after the country's women's team had dispatched France 58-4.

Veteran Rhyse Martin began his farewell tournament in style, scoring a try and going perfect from seven conversions against a dogged Lebanon outfit.

His try with nine minutes left on the clock finished off the Cedars, who were fading in humid conditions.

But Lebanon never stopped trying, with fullback Jacob Kiraz (207 metres) and winger Tony Frances (292 metres) constant threats in attack, while Wests Tigers stalwart Alex Twal led the defence with 48 tackles.

Winger Naomi Kelly crossed four times in the women's game as the Orchids ran in 12 tries to one.

England ended the day's women's action in comprehensive fashion against Wales, with Connie Boyd and Anna Davies both scoring hat-tricks in the 70-6 rout in Perth.

AAP/ABC

Tech.title: Video game ownership bill introduced in Congress
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York’s 15th congressional district in the Bronx introduced the Power To The Players Act this week. If passed, the bill would direct the Federal Trade Commission to establish regulations that guarantee consumers ownership of a game when they pay for it, rather than a licensing agreement.

It’s increasingly common for games sold to require a connection to a server. Meaning that when a company decides to shut down those servers, the games often become unplayable. Rep. Torres singles out NBA 2K25 as a recent example. 2K will be delisting the game from storefronts at the end of the month and shutting down its servers on December 31st, limiting its playability.

Concerns around ownership, the ability to play, resell, or transfer games have drawn attention recently following Sony’s announcement that it planned to phase out physical game discs in 2028. In a statement announcing the bill, Rep. Torres said, “A game that can be taken away the moment a company pulls the plug is not a purchase. It is a rental disguised as a sale.”

The bill would not only give players ownership of a game, “rather than a license to play it,” but also require developers to institute an offline mode before shutting down supporting servers. That is similar to the Protect Our Games Act introduced by State Sen. John Kane in Pennsylvania, which would require companies to provide an offline gaming mode, an online gaming mode independent of the company’s servers, or a minimum 25 percent refund when titles are being sunset.

Tech.title: Lenovo’s fast, comfy SteamOS handheld is hundreds off
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Legion Go S with SteamOS is a pretty solid alternative to the $789 Steam Deck OLED. It runs identical software, but ships in a design with two-stage triggers, a bigger eight-inch IPS screen (1080p and up to 120Hz versus 800p and 90Hz in the Deck OLED), and it’s got double the RAM and storage (32GB and 1TB, respectively), not to mention a slightly faster processor in the Ryzen Z1 Extreme.

At $999.99, its current discounted price at Best Buy, it’s worth considering if you’re deciding on a handheld. The Legion Go S is not as powerful as the $1,299.99 Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 that just launched, which has the Z2 Extreme and a OLED screen, but it’s no slouch, either.

This model launched with Windows 11 and the Ryzen Z2 Go. Despite being a newer chip, it’s less powerful than the Z1 Extreme in the discounted model. SteamOS and the faster internals within this configuration will provide a better experience. Check out my colleague Sean Hollister’s review of multiple configs of the Go S, and see how it stacks up in his benchmarks.

Tech.title: J Mascis has nothing better to do
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Dinosaur Jr. frontman J Mascis is known as something of a slacker guitar god. He stands stoically onstage, barely moving, as he seemingly effortlessly works through deft guitar solos and lopsided riffs. Unfortunately, Mascis has developed a similar reputation as an interview subject, quietly sitting and offering deft nonanswers.

That’s not to say that Mascis can’t be funny or charming. As our interview was winding down and I was thanking him for his time, he started to loosen up a bit. He told me about his youth as a mini golf “enthusiast.” “I had a 3-foot putt for the win” at a mini-golf tournament, he said, but “that’s when I realized that I was a choker … When I was 11, I choked.” And that’s when he decided, “I should maybe not do sports.” So, instead of becoming a professional mini golfer, Mascis went on to form one of the most important bands in alternative rock.

While most of his contemporaries have called it quits or are just going through the motions onstage for a paycheck, the original lineup of Mascis, bassist Lou Barlow, and drummer Patrick Murphy are still regularly putting out new LPs of reliable rockers. But Mascis says there isn’t any grand secret to the band’s longevity. Over 40 years deep, he says, “I guess we have nothing better to do.”

What, for an interviewer, can come off as frustrating indifference might actually be the key to Mascis’ staying power — for better or worse. Creatively and professionally, his modus operandi seems to be rolling with the punches and not overthinking things.

For the new record There Near, he said, the band “just didn’t push it.” There were no eight-hour marathon studio sessions. They weren’t meticulously fine-tuning basslines or trading Logic sessions back and forth remotely. Mascis would roll in with fully prepared demos and the band would immediately start recording, even as Barlow and Murph were still learning their parts, “on the off chance that it comes together quickly.”

The same sort of relaxed approach also informs Mascis’ gear choices. He said, “I am kind of a tube purist guy, but it’s just also kind of inconvenient sometimes,” so he uses whatever works. That means while he mixes and masters to tape, he’s also tracking in Pro Tools.

When it comes to designing signature instruments with Fender, he’s just as easygoing. “I try to, you know, do the important things that I want, but not make it too complicated … I think it’s better to keep it kind of cheap … just so people can do what they want with it.” The neck is his biggest concern, he said. “I’m a sucker for jumbo frets and, you know, if the neck is good and the frets and stuff, that’s the main thing. Most of the other stuff, you know, you can swap out if you want.”

But that somewhat lackadaisical attitude has also caught him some heat. Two years ago, Mascis released a video for his solo track “Old Friends” that was made using generative AI. Speaking with The Verge, he finally publicly addressed the controversy. “Yeah, just some kid did it,” he said. “I thought it looked cool, so… Yeah, that’s dipping my toes into the... I don’t do much with videos.” He trailed off repeatedly while answering before finally admitting, “But yeah, I guess that’s a slippery slope.”

Similarly, he said that while he doesn’t believe there is a place for AI in music making, we have to acknowledge that it’s here whether we like it or not, and “I guess we’re learning how to deal with it. And hopefully it won’t kill us all.”

About the only thing that Mascis could muster strong feelings about was the band’s infamously loud live shows. (Dinosaur Jr.’s recent performance at the tiny Baby’s All Right is what finally convinced me to start packing earplugs.) “I noticed the audience too seems more desperate for something kind of reality-based,” he said, letting a touch of his purist heart show. “We don’t have in-ear monitors or click tracks. We have amps and you know, just, I think some people are responding to the reality of it. Like they really need something that’s not, you know, computer-generated or something.”

He bemoaned the lack of amps onstage (Mascis plays in front of three full stacks, even in a 280-person-capacity club) and the reliance on high-tech front-of-house setups. “It’s very weird. Now, soundmen create the sound instead of capture the sound,” he said. Of course, his recognition of the visceral power of live music and directly connecting with an audience makes his indifference to AI all the more baffling.

Dinosaur Jr. are currently touring the US behind There Near, which is out now.

Tech.title: Trump says Google kisses his ass
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

During a rally on Saturday, October 17th, in Highland Heights, Kentucky, Donald Trump bragged about how much more powerful and influential he was during his second term. While listing off his accomplishments, he mentioned his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario.

“This is a much more powerful term. I can do stuff that’s unbelievable … I called Google, Google Maps. See, Google wouldn’t have taken my call in the first term. Now they kiss my ass.”

Trump seems to be implying that he convinced Google to reflect the name change personally. That would seem to contradict Google’s statement on the matter, in which it said that it simply reflects “official government sources, which is GNIS for the US … These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country.”

Throughout his second term, however, Silicon Valley — including Google and its CEO Sundar Pichai — has gone out of its way to try and ingratiate itself with President Trump, lavishing him with gifts, compliments, and donations to his pet projects. Google did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tech.title: The best gadget I bought this year is a milk frother
Tech.content:
is a reporter who writes about tech, money, and human behavior. She joined The Verge in 2014 as science editor. Previously, she was a reporter at Bloomberg.

Back in February, I went to Los Angeles to take in some art and stayed in Koreatown. Down the street from my hotel, there was this little coffee shop — Stagger — that is, I think, best known for its matcha, which is good. But the drink I unexpectedly found myself obsessed with was their cream top, an iced Americano with, yep, vanilla cream on top. When I got back to Oakland, I kept thinking about how badly I wanted one.

For more than 20 years, I’ve been drinking my coffee — iced or otherwise — black. Originally this was because I knew I could put black coffee that had cooled off in the microwave to reheat it without worrying that the milk in it would curdle. (Gross, I know.) Then, as I started drinking better coffee, it felt like the best way to appreciate the expensive beans I was buying.

So my attachment to the cream top surprised me. And then, when Oakland had a gnarly heat wave in March, I decided there was one way I’d tolerate it: fancy coffee drinks. I splashed out $14 for the Zulay Kitchen frother and I was off.

A handheld foamer looks and works kinda like an immersion blender. I pour milk into a glass, stick the frother in there, and then hold the power button until it reaches my preferred consistency. When the disposable batteries it uses are fresh, this takes about 30 seconds to a minute. As the batteries degrade, it takes longer; if I’m getting impatient about how long it’s taking me to make my frothy treats, it’s time to change the batteries. The frother also works to beat eggs, mix protein powder or creatine into a drink, and make hot chocolate. But by far it’s gotten the most use making my coffee drinks as I set out to make a cream top of my own.

Also I think it’s neat to watch the foam descend into the coffee. Photo: Elizabeth Lopatto / The Verge

The cream top descended from the Einspänner, an espresso drink that’s named for a one-horse carriage. The original Viennese version used hot espresso, and the whipped cream on top served as a kind of insulation, which kept the drivers’ drinks hot for them when they were out in the cold. (Obviously, its popularity expanded beyond carriage drivers.) It isn’t clear to me how the Einspänner made it to South Korea, but it exploded in popularity there, with all kinds of variations, mostly iced. And then from South Korea, it made its way to the US, where the ground had already been cleared by Starbucks’ “cold foam” drinks.

The notable thing about the cream top, besides the addition of delicious fat and sugar to coffee, was that the cream wasn’t as light as latte foam, but wasn’t as heavy as ordinary whipped cream. It was melty and dripped slowly into the coffee.

My first experiments with my at-home cream top were pretty simple. I don’t have an espresso machine, but I do make concentrated cold brew in hot weather, which has a strong enough flavor to stand up against the foam. (Some recipes suggest powdered espresso if you don’t want to use concentrated cold brew.)

After I mastered the simple cream top, I began making forays into weirder breakfast treats, my favorite of which I… recreated from a Starbucks ad. It’s a cold brew with coconut ube cold foam, the top of which I dust with toasted coconut flakes. It is dank. (This is a recipe for a more sophisticated version than I make.) So when it was 90 degrees in Oakland for about two weeks running recently, this drink was how I consoled myself.

To be honest, I’m just recommending getting a frother. You can spend a lot on a milk frother and some people do. I relied on America’s Test Kitchen to steer me in the right direction — but outlets like Wirecutter and Bon Appétit have their own preferred options. This one is cheap and simple, and it’s been treating me right. I’m sure the Apple HomeView is nice, too, but in pleasure per dollar can it match a $14 cold foamer that takes AA batteries? I have my doubts.

Tech.title: How overhead projectors took over your classroom
Tech.content:
It used to be so easy to get away with things in school. The teacher, after all, was always turned around writing at the chalkboard! But then came a bit of technology, previously mostly used for military purposes, called the overhead projector. It would change far more than just the disciplinary record of students everywhere.

In this episode of Version History, we tell the story of the overhead projector. David Pierce is joined by The Verge’s Jake Kastrenakes and Stanford professor Antero Garcia to discuss how overhead projectors were developed, how they made their way into classrooms, and how they changed so much about the way kids learn. They also try to figure out why overhead projectors have mostly gone away, and whether the things that replaced them — from PowerPoint presentations to computer screens to those new-fangled smart boards — actually improved on the OHP.

This is the final episode of the fifth season of Version History, all about the most iconic school tech. Thanks so much for watching, listening, sending feedback, and everything else! Other than the OHP, we also spent this season looking at Oregon Trail, the original Chromebook, the One Laptop Per Child program, the LeapFrog LeapPad, and those ubiquitous Texas Instruments calculators. Tech.title: Cities want to put the boot on robotaxis
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on autonomous vehicles, policy, and road rules, follow Andrew J. Hawkins. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

The first state to pass a law legalizing self-driving cars operating on public roads was Nevada in June 2011 — long before such vehicles were operating on public roads. This was three years before the introduction of Tesla’s Autopilot, five years before Waymo spun out of the Google self-driving car project, and seven years before the first commercial robotaxi service got underway (in Arizona, not Nevada). Nevada was ahead of the curve primarily due to lobbying: Google saw Nevada as prime testing ground for its prototypes, so it urged lawmakers to pass the law that allowed it to do so. The legislation even included a provision exempting drivers from text-messaging bans while the automated system was engaged.

Back then, many states and cities welcomed self-driving cars with open arms, eager to be seen as future-forward and pro-innovation. They had no inkling that over a decade later, they would be back at the drafting table crafting legislation to rein in these same self-driving cars.

While federal regulators scramble to establish safety standards, legislation that would establish rules for autonomous vehicles remains stalled in Congress — and has been for years. Washington’s paralysis has left local lawmakers to create their own playbooks to ensure robot cars at least follow some rules of the road.

The result is a patchwork of rules and regulations for robotaxi operators to follow — an outcome that many industry leaders were desperate to avoid. And as robotaxis continue to spread to new cities, local officials are discovering more unintended consequences of their new robot residents, leading to even more rules and an ever-growing patchwork of complexity for operators.

How it’s going

Municipalities generally lack authority over vehicle manufacturing standards, but they hold broad authority over street operations. As such, they’ve been using that authority to pass their own laws governing the rollout of robotaxis. There’s not an exact count of the number of local regulations and ordinances that have been passed since robotaxis have gone mainstream. But in the absence of any federal rules, cities and states have been flexing their authority in an effort to bring order to some of the chaos.

Minneapolis is considering an ordinance to require human monitors inside autonomous vehicles, which would effectively ban driverless operations. The San Diego City Council passed a resolution seeking to block Waymo from the airport and give local agencies direct control over AVs in emergencies. And Austin firefighters have expressed concern over the Tesla Cybercab’s lack of steering wheel or pedals, which they argue could lead to issues if first responders need to move a stalled vehicle. They want to require AV developers to establish dedicated, rapid-response towing protocols and direct human operator communications for emergency situations.

It’s not just cities or blue states taking a harder line, either — the pushback is blurring traditional political lines. It used to be the case that Republicans were seen as more welcoming of autonomous vehicles, while Democrats were seen as more skeptical. This has certainly borne out in a handful of Democrat-led cities — New York City, Chicago, Washington, DC — that still haven’t legalized driverless cars. But now even some red states are considering tightening the leash, including Kentucky, Oklahoma, South Dakota, and Iowa.

Even in tech-friendly California, state lawmakers are mulling ways to bring robotaxis to heel. Several bills have been introduced to give cities direct authority to limit AV fleet sizes, restrict operating hours, or enact local permit bans within municipal limits. Additionally, emergency protocols were drafted to require AV companies to give local police and fire departments physical override access or emergency remote shut-off mechanisms.

Some municipalities are flexing their land-use and zoning powers to crack down on robot cars. Culver City explored emergency moratoriums on building permits for AV fleet facilities, while Santa Monica used local noise and traffic ordinances to restrict 24-hour charging hubs. It would seem that even robotaxis aren’t immune to NIMBY complaints.

What happens next

As the local debate over autonomous vehicles intensifies, AV developers are increasingly looking overseas as a potential hedge to more obstacles in cropping up in the US. Waymo is planning to expand its service in London, Tokyo, and Munich. Uber is teeing up vehicles for Manchester, Madrid, and Dubai. If the US is getting too complex and over-regulated, perhaps they can find friendlier reception elsewhere.

Still, the US presents the industry’s best chances of turning a profit, especially as costs for developers continue to grow. Rather than fighting strict local regulations head-on, companies like Waymo, Zoox, and Aurora are prioritizing states with explicit legislative preemption that prevents individual cities from banning the technology. And at the national level, industry trade groups like the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association are aggressively pushing for more preemption powers in an attempt to create more unified standards.

Congress may eventually get around to passing high-level safety legislation, but it’s highly unlikely that any bill passed at the federal level would seek to strip cities of their core police, zoning, and emergency response powers. States will also have a say, and sometimes that may complement or conflict with their own cities. Even airport authorities are getting in on the action, proposing their own slate of rules for robotaxis. AV companies would be well advised to get used to the patchwork — it’s not going anywhere.

By the way

Even if the feds pass a sweeping national framework, like the proposed SELF DRIVE Act, cities and states would still keep their authority over local road usage. In other words, cities are going to be the main arbiters of robotaxi permission for the foreseeable future.

Texas may be the Wild West, with fewer rules governing self-driving cars than most states, but California is still the gold standard. Securing a deployment permit from the California Public Utilities Commission, for example, is viewed by the industry as a definitive safety validation.

Read this

Streetsblog reports that Uber and Waymo have spent more than $15 million on lobbying state officials in New York.

Tesla had to change the name of its Full Self-Driving software to “Assisted Driving” to win approval from European Union regulators, Reuters reports

Tesla provided first responders in Austin three days of training and emergency guidebooks on how to interact with its Cybercabs, according to The Daily Texan

Tech.title: TikTok bans Musk documentary account
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just ahead of the wider release of Alex Gibney’s Musk documentary, TikTok has banned the film’s social media account from its platform. TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment. According to The Hollywood Reporter, the film’s distributor, Bleecker Street, was informed Friday afternoon that a “permanent suspension” was imminent. Bleecker Street has not yet responded to a request for comment from The Verge.

While TikTok has no official affiliation with Elon Musk, part owner Larry Ellison appears in the film via a text message offering to help Musk fund his Twitter purchase.

Last month, YouTube, Meta, X, and TikTok all faced backlash for rejecting ads for the film. YouTube and Meta quickly reversed course, calling it an “error.” However, TikTok and X have refused to change their stance, and neither platform has allowed paid s for the film.

Banning the documentary’s account, however, marks a serious escalation, and one laced with a dash of irony — shortly before the account was removed, it posted that people should see the movie “before it gets shut down.”

The irony. Screenshot: The Hollywood Reporter

Tech.title: Disney agrees to hire the majority of Character.AI’s workforce
Tech.content:
In Brief

After chatbot startup Character.AI filed for bankruptcy earlier this week, many of its employees will have the opportunity to take jobs at Disney.

Character.AI’s former CEO Karandeep Anand recently became the entertainment giant’s first CTO, and the startup previously said that Disney had agreed to acquire some of its assets for $20 million.

A legal filing spotted by Bloomberg revealed more details about the agreement between Character.AI and Disney, with Disney agreeing to make employment offers to at least 60 Character.AI employees — the majority of the workforce — paying them an estimated $60 million in annual compensation.

The filing also says that the “vast majority” of Character.AI employees who were offered jobs at Disney accepted them. However, this is a stalking horse bid, so another company could come forward with a higher offer.

The filing says that despite its “large and engaged user base,” Character.AI has been hobbled by high costs and “potential litigation-related liabilities and regulatory engagement.” (The company was sued by the mother of a 14-year-old boy who said her son became obsessed with one of Character.AI’s chatbots before committing suicide; it also faces government investigations over child safety concerns.)

Tech.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Rivian’s next act
Tech.content:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility!

As I wrapped my TechCrunch Disrupt interview with Rivian CEO and founder RJ Scaringe, I kept circling back to one question: What does Scaringe want Rivian to become? If you look at Rivian’s moves over the past year, it’s clear that Scaringe wants the company to be much more than an EV maker. But he doesn’t want to stray completely from that mission either.

Rivian is far more vertically integrated than it was just a couple of years ago. It has developed its own AI models to power its in-vehicle assistant and is building an end-to-end automated driving stack for its passenger vehicles and future robotaxis through a partnership with Uber. It’s even developing custom silicon, a 5 nm processor in collaboration with Arm and TSMC. And then there is its $5.8 billion joint technology venture with VW Group focused on electric architecture and software.

Scaringe’s ambitions extend beyond Rivian as well, although there is always a link back. He created a micromobility skunkworks program that has since spun out into a startup called Also. And he founded an industrial robotics startup called Mind Robotics, which is now 31% owned by Rivian and counts the automaker as a prospective customer. (Scaringe announced onstage that former Ford, Apple, and Tesla executive Doug Field has been hired as president of Mind Robotics.)

Scaringe’s aspirations were on display as he talked of not only expanding the joint venture with VW to cover AI and autonomy, but also licensing Rivian’s tech to “many different brands.”

So what does Rivian look like at the end of the decade? Certainly not just a maker of electric trucks and SUVs. The term I kept coming back to was “tech supplier.”

Hear me out. Rivian is clearing a path toward licensing its electric architecture and software as well as its AI models and autonomy stack. Meanwhile, the Mind Robotics startup it partially owns is building industrial robots to not only be used in Rivian factories, but also sold to other companies. Then there’s the robotaxi business. A successful launch with Uber could open the door to more deals.

And Scaringe is already imagining how autonomy could reshape Rivian’s own vehicles.

“Where it gets really interesting is then you think beyond R2 and R3 and start to imagine the form factors that you want to build for a personally owned autonomous vehicle. You know, it opens up all kinds of design opportunities. It can create dramatically different experiences,” he said in an interview with TechCrunch. “I’m wildly excited about what the next 10 years look like in transportation because of what this enables us to dream and think about.”

Deals!

Image Credits:Bryce Durbin

Bedrock Robotics, a startup developing autonomous driving tech for construction vehicles, is raising $600 million, Axios reported, citing sources.

Dot Ai completed its acquisition of electric vehicle car-sharing business Envoy Technologies in a $65 million all-stock transaction, according to a regulatory filing.

Evos, a startup that developed AI agents to automate work for industrial businesses, including freight brokerages, raised $9 million in a pre-seed round co-led by Uncork Capital and Field Ventures.

Mana Battery, a Colorado-based startup developing anode-free sodium batteries, raised $10.15 million in a round led by Voyager Ventures.

PlusAI, the autonomous trucking developer, and Texas Ventures Acquisition III filed a Form S-4 registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission —advancing its previously announced agreement to go public via a merger with a blank-check company.

Volvo is leveling up its automated driving system through an expansion of its nearly decade-long partnership with Nvidia. Neither company shared financial terms of the deal. Tech.title: Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns
Tech.content:
In Brief

Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab, this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)

However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

Tech.title: TikTok permanently bans ‘Musk’ documentary advertising account
Tech.content:
In Brief

A four-hour documentary about Elon Musk continues to meet resistance from social media platforms, with TikTok banning the film’s advertising account.

According to a story in The Hollywood Reporter, the documentary’s distributor Bleecker Street was recently notified by TikTok that the account had received a “permanent suspension” due to its political content. TechCrunch has reached out to TikTok for comment.

Ads promoting the trailer for “Musk” — directed by Oscar-winner filmmaker Alex Gibney — were initially rejected by Meta and YouTube as well, though those platforms eventually allowed the ad, with Meta blaming the rejection on “an error.” Gibney recently confirmed that the film’s international distributor Universal had wavered in its plans to release “Musk,” though it’s now moving forward.

X, which Musk owns, has refused to carry ads for “Musk.” TikTok’s U.S. operations are partly owned by Larry Ellison — who, like Musk, has been a notable supporter of President Donald Trump.

“Musk” opened in just four theaters last weekend and is now rolling out more broadly. Next year, it’s supposed to stream on HBO — now part of Paramount/Skydance and led by Ellison’s son David.

Tech.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
Tech.content:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

Tech.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
Tech.content:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost. Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.

“I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch. It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance. And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.”

It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.

After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default. This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform. That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s.

“Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.”

Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however. One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website, blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago. For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment. Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue.

“We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.”

Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures.

“In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization. And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.”

This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT. It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI. Its title has been updated, as well.

Tech.title: Ember’s new temperature-controlled mug makes my nightly tea ritual even better
Tech.content:
With the nights getting chillier, I’ve been reaching for a cup of tea more often. And if there’s one thing that can make a cozy fall night even better, it’s a warm drink that actually stays warm. Enter Ember’s new Mug 3, the latest version of the company’s temperature-controlled smart mug, which is designed to keep your drink at just the right temperature for as long as you sip.

Ember first introduced its smart mug in 2016 to solve a problem most coffee and tea drinkers know all too well: getting distracted for a few minutes, only to return to a lukewarm drink. Now, the company is back with its third-generation mug, which brings a handful of practical upgrades.

The biggest change is that you no longer have to open the app to adjust your drink’s temperature. Instead, you can use the button on the bottom of the mug to cycle through five preset temperatures, starting at 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Each press raises the temperature by five degrees, up to a maximum of 145 degrees, so you can easily make your drink a little hotter with each click.

Honestly, this is the feature I ended up using the most during my time testing out the mug. At night, when I’m curled up in bed with a book and a cup of tea, my phone is usually somewhere across the room. Being able to adjust my drink without getting up to find it is a small convenience, but one I genuinely appreciate.

It’s also a welcome change for users who have reported running into connectivity or pairing issues with the Ember app.

That said, I do have one complaint: the button is located on the bottom of the mug. It’s a peculiar design choice when you’re dealing with a cup full of hot liquid, and it isn’t particularly easy to press, either. I often found myself tilting the mug and pressing down firmly to get it to respond. So, while I appreciate the addition of on-mug controls, I wish Ember had made the button easier to reach.

If you prefer using your phone, the Ember app still offers plenty of customization. After pairing the mug with your phone over Bluetooth, you can choose presets based on what you’re drinking. Ember recommends 136 degrees Fahrenheit for black coffee, 132 degrees for green tea, and 142 degrees for lemon water. You can also create your own temperature presets, which is handy if you like your drinks a little hotter or cooler than the recommended settings.

Image Credits:Ember

The Mug 3 also comes with a few other upgrades, including a sliding lid designed to help prevent spills. The mug can also keep your drink at its desired temperature for up to three hours on a single charge. And it’s the first mug in Ember’s lineup to be top-rack dishwasher-safe, making cleanup easier. (Just keep in mind that it isn’t microwave-safe.)

The Ember Mug 3 comes in two sizes: a 10-ounce model for $129 and a 14-ounce version for $149.

The smaller mug is available in black, white, and stainless steel, while the larger size comes in eight colors, including sage green, lavender, powder blue, salt blue, sandstone, white, black, and matcha green.

Alongside the new mug, Ember also introduced the Tumbler 2, which replaces both the Travel Mug 2 and the original Tumbler in its lineup. The 16-ounce tumbler features a slimmer, taller design intended to fit standard car cup holders. It’s available in black for $179, while the Travel Mug 2 will remain available until supplies run out.

The products are available to purchase on Ember’s website, Target, and Amazon.

Tech.title: Mark Wahlberg wants to take on the longevity-startup crowd with an affordable gym concept
Tech.content:
Mark Wahlberg has started companies of his own and backed plenty of others. But he says the gym he’s opening in December has him more excited than anything he’s done in his entire career. It also goes after a corner of the market where venture money keeps flowing: pricey, diagnostics-heavy wellness.

Speaking with us at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, the actor said the first Municipal Gym opens in December. It’s a 32,000-square-foot club outside Las Vegas with blood work, epigenetic testing, recovery gear, compression therapy, cold plunges, and a café that serves up protein muffins, among other things. He’s pitching it as the affordable alternative to the longevity clubs that charge tens of thousands of dollars a year for much the same thing.

It’s the second part of a scheme that was, in some ways, first hatched seven years ago with a casual sportswear line.

The clothing brand Municipal launched during COVID, which Wahlberg freely volunteered “was not a good idea,” given that clothing was a lousy business to enter in 2020, with retailers from J.Crew to Brooks Brothers going bankrupt.

It grew out of what he’d been seeing as a celebrity fitness spokesperson. He’d done collabs with various brands, and other companies kept approaching him to be their brand ambassador, but they all seemed to want the same thing, he said. “Everybody just kind of wanted to sell T-shirts and sneakers. And I was like, well, I want to kind of have a bigger impact on people’s lives as a whole.”

By that, he meant what people eat, what supplements they take, how they train, and how they recover. “We figured, okay, we’ll start in the apparel space, and then we’ll build from there.” He says he only takes swings at “things that I’m very passionate about and things that are a direct extension of who I am.”

Even without a pandemic, clothing is a brutal business, as we pointed out, citing Lululemon’s repeated quality-control challenges. But Wahlberg didn’t seem fazed, talking instead about why the gym fits his vision. He thought it “always could be great for the brand” in part because it gives people a place to “actually feel and touch the clothes” before they buy. Besides, he continued, how people exercise is “another big part of people’s lives.”

Most in the space have been laser-focused on the high end. Fountain Life, the longevity company co-founded by Tony Robbins, raised $18 million last year to expand its centers for wealthy clients, and a full subscription runs $21,500 a year, according to reports. The Estate, a company co-founded by Robbins and hospitality executive Sam Nazarian, is still mapping out plans to charge $35,000 memberships to its wellness centers. Equinox is similarly building a waitlist for a $36,000 longevity add-on that it plans to launch atop a traditional gym membership.

Wahlberg says Municipal aims for that same luxury tier but for a lot less. “We have a better price point than our competitors, and we’re going to get far more results,” he said. For $99, he said as an example, members will receive three rounds of blood work and an hour with a doctor to flag what they’re predisposed to. Supplements and hormone therapy are also “right there.”

When we asked whether the gyms will double as storefronts for his other products (he owns a supplements brand, for example), he said “kind of.” What he’s really building, he said, is a “health and wellness ecosystem” with “everything there, soup to nuts.”

He didn’t put a number on how many gyms he wants, but he called the growth strategy “aggressive,” telling us that “landlords and developers who toured the Las Vegas site have offered “AAA locations at very favorable terms, with great TI” (tenant-improvement allowances that help pay for the build-out).

Wahlberg’s last big bet on a gym chain might have scared off someone else. We told him we’d recently watched “Wahl Street,” his reality show, in which an early episode shows him getting deeply involved with the fitness chain F45 in 2019, and that we wanted to warn him about what was coming. “How did you know about the pandemic?” he joked, to laughs from the crowd. He bought into the company, known for its 45-minute classes, at a $450 million valuation. It went public in 2021, then was delisted from the NYSE in 2023 after its stock collapsed. Wahlberg said he learned a lot from the experience.

“I think the biggest takeaway was just making sure that I’m involved with people that share the same approach that I do.” He also said he always thought big box was the better model. F45’s classes suit people who are short on time, but he wants members to hang around Municipal for hours. Plenty of gyms run on a “join up but don’t show up” model, he said, adding, “I can’t understand that philosophy.”

The name Municipal is very intentional and clearly means a lot to Wahlberg, who grew up poor in Boston, one of nine kids, playing on public basketball courts and golf courses. “You learn a lot on the blacktop,” he said. “You learn to win, to lose, to compete, and hopefully to get back up and do it again.”

He has never hidden his rough youth. (He was sentenced to two years for assaults as a teenager and served 45 days.)

In fact, earlier in the afternoon on Thursday, surrounded by friends and business associates in a seating area backstage at Disrupt — this is the man who inspired the show “Entourage,” after all — he said he was turned around by two people, including Father Jim Flavin, a Boston-area parish priest who has been in Wahlberg’s life since he was 13.

He wants the gyms to carry that same spirit. “It’s a place to work, but have fun and support each other and create community and really challenge people to be better versions of themselves,” he said. “I’ve come from next to nothing to being in an amazing position,” Wahlberg continued. “I try to constantly remind myself that I can inspire other people growing up in similar situations, especially inner-city kids and at-risk youth, that there is a way to overcome your circumstances if you’re willing to go out there and do the work.”

At 55, his goals have changed, naturally. While he was once focused on looking good, “I just want to feel good when I wake up in the morning,” he said. “I want to be able to conquer all the things that I have planned for the day.”

He also said his plate is exceedingly full right now, between the gym, a film role as Pete Rose, and his daughter’s equestrian career. He’s so eager for the gym to open, he said, that visiting the construction site feels like “literally watching paint dry.” Indeed, asked if he was open to taking on new ventures, he shrugged. “I’m not out there hunting, looking for the next thing for sure.” But he wouldn’t rule it out, he added quickly. “If something amazing were to come along, obviously I wouldn’t turn it down.”

Pictured above with Walhberg, friend and business partner Bruce K. Lee.
